units.title: Sentence structure & word order
units.intro: English is S-V-O. Tigrinya is S-O-V, so keep the verb in the middle and never leave out the linking verb (is/are/was/were).

cards.title: S-V-O vs S-O-V
rule: English declarative order is **Subject–Verb–Object**.
Tigrinya is **Subject–Object–Verb**; putting the English verb last is a common mistake from Tigrinya.
Keep the main verb as a **middle anchor** after the subject.

examples.text: The guard locked the gate at midnight.
The guard the gate locked at midnight.
examples.fix: The guard locked the gate at midnight.
The guard locked the gate.

cards.pattern: S + V + O

cards.title: Why the verb goes in the middle
body: In English the position of a word shows its job. The noun **before** the verb is the doer (subject) and the noun **after** the verb is the receiver (object): *The dog bit the boy* and *The boy bit the dog* mean different things only because of word order.
Tigrinya puts the verb at the end (literally "I letter read"). If you translate word for word you get **S-O-V** English, which is wrong: ✗ *I the letter read* → **I read the letter**.

A quick test: underline the subject, then check that the very next part is the verb (with its auxiliaries): *The students **have finished** their project.* Time and place phrases usually go at the end: *We met our teacher **in the market yesterday**.*
Questions are the main exception: an auxiliary comes before the subject (*Did you finish?*), but the main verb still comes before the object.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The guard the gate locked at midnight."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** English declarative order is **Subject–Verb–Object**.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The guard the gate locked at midnight." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The guard locked the gate at midnight."
**Check:** Tigrinya is **Subject–Object–Verb**; putting the English verb last is a common mistake from Tigrinya.
**Same pattern:** "Locked the guard the gate." → "The guard locked the gate."

cards.answer: The guard locked the gate at midnight.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence with correct word order.

options.A: Our team the regional final won last year.
options.B: Won our team the regional final last year.
options.C: Our team won the regional final last year.
options.D: Our team last year the regional final won.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The subject is "Our team" and the verb is "won".

**Step 2:** The object "the regional final" follows the verb; the time phrase goes last.

**Step 3:** Only option C is S-V-O.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "The boy kicked the ball." What is the object?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The object receives the action and normally comes after the verb.

**Step 2:** "the ball" is what was kicked.

**Step 3:** "the boy" is the subject; "kicked" is the verb.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence shows a Tigrinya word-order mistake?

options.A: Every morning my mother makes injera.
options.B: My mother injera every morning makes.
options.D: My mother makes injera every morning.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Tigrinya puts the verb last (S-O-V).

**Step 2:** "My mother injera every morning makes" copies that order.

**Step 3:** The other sentences keep the verb after the subject.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Linking verbs and clause boundaries
rule: English always needs a **linking verb** (*is/are/was/were*) between the subject and the word that describes it: *She **is** a teacher.*
Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splice).
Use a full stop, semicolon, or a conjunction (*and/but/so/because*).

examples.fix: She is a teacher.

examples.text: It rained; therefore we stayed in.

cards.title: Linking verbs and sentence boundaries
body: A **linking verb** connects the subject to a description: *be, become, seem, look, feel*. Tigrinya can drop or attach the linking verb, but English always needs it: ✗ *She a nurse* → **She is a nurse**; ✗ *The soup hot* → **The soup is hot**.
A **clause boundary** is where one complete idea ends. Two complete ideas cannot be joined by a comma alone (a *comma splice*): ✗ *I was hungry, I ate*.

Four correct ways to fix a comma splice: (1) full stop: *I was hungry. I ate.* (2) semicolon: *I was hungry; I ate.* (3) comma + FANBOYS: *I was hungry, so I ate.* (4) subordinator: *Because I was hungry, I ate.*
Watch long subjects: *The books on the top shelf **are** old* – the linking verb agrees with "books", not "shelf".

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She a teacher."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** English needs a linking verb (*is/are/was/were*) between subject and complement.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She a teacher." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She is a teacher."
**Check:** Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splice).

cards.title: Linking verbs and helping verbs
rule: A **linking verb** joins the subject to a word that **describes or names** it. Nothing is "done": *Aster **is** a nurse. The soup **smells** good. He **became** a doctor.*
Common linking verbs: **be** (am/is/are/was/were), **become, seem, look, feel, sound, smell, taste, appear, get, grow, remain, stay**.

A **helping verb** helps a main verb to make a tense, a question, a negative or the passive: *She **is** working. They **have** finished. **Do** you agree? The road **was** built.* Helping verbs: **be, have, do** and the modals (**can, will, must, should**…).
The same word can do both jobs. Ask: is there another (main) verb after it? *She **is** tired* – no other verb → **linking verb**. *She **is** sleeping* – main verb *sleeping* → **helping verb**.
After a linking verb use an **adjective**, not an adverb: *The food tastes **good*** (not *well*). *She looks **happy*** (not *happily*).
English never leaves out the linking verb: ✗ *My brother a farmer.* → ✔ *My brother **is** a farmer.*

examples.text: My brother is a hardworking farmer.

examples.fix: My brother is a hardworking farmer.
The injera tastes good.
She is working in the garden.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence uses 'looks' as a linking verb?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A linking verb is followed by a word that describes the subject.

**Step 2:** In B, *tired* describes *she* → *looks* is a linking verb (= seems).

**Step 3:** In A, C and D, *looks at / for / through* is an action (using your eyes or searching).

**Tip:** Is there another verb after it? No → linking verb (She is tired). Yes → helping verb (She is sleeping).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In 'They have finished the work', the word 'have' is ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** There is another verb after *have*: *finished*.

**Step 2:** *have* helps *finished* make the present perfect → **helping verb**.

**Step 3:** In *They have a car*, *have* would be a main verb (= own).

**Tip:** Is there another verb after it? No → linking verb (She is tired). Yes → helping verb (She is sleeping).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correct sentence.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *smell* here is a linking verb: it describes the flowers.

**Step 2:** After a linking verb use an **adjective**: *beautiful*.

**Step 3:** C has the verb at the end (S-O-V); D has no finite verb.

**Tip:** look / smell / taste / sound / feel + adjective.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence is correct?

options.A: The weather very is hot in Massawa.
options.B: Very hot the weather in Massawa.
options.C: The weather very hot in Massawa.
options.D: The weather is very hot in Massawa.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A subject + adjective needs a linking verb.

**Step 2:** "is" must come between "The weather" and "very hot".

**Step 3:** The other sentences omit it or misplace it.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How can you correct "He missed the bus, he was late"?

options.A: He missed, the bus he was late.
options.B: He missed the bus, he late.
options.C: He missed the bus, so he was late.
options.D: He missed the bus he was late.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The original is a comma splice: two independent clauses joined by a comma.

**Step 2:** Adding "so" after the comma joins them correctly and shows result.

**Step 3:** Option D removes the comma but is still a run-on sentence.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence without an error.

options.A: I was tired; however, I finished the work.
options.B: I tired, but I finished the work.
options.C: I was tired however, I finished the work.
options.D: I was tired, however I finished the work.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "however" joins clauses with a semicolon before and a comma after.

**Step 2:** Option B is a comma splice; C misses the linking verb "was"; D puts the comma in the wrong place.

**Step 3:** Only the first option is correct.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

Identify the sentence that contains a linking verb

options.A: The security guard the main gate locked at midnight.
options.B: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.
options.C: At midnight the security guard the main gate locked.
options.D: Locked the security guard the main gate at midnight.

why: Answer B: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.
English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object (S-V-O) pattern. The subject is 'The security guard', the verb is 'locked', and the direct object is 'the main gate'.

Option A and Option C place the verb ('locked') at the end of the clause, which is an S-O-V pattern typical of Tigrinya grammar (ሓላው ሰላም ማዕጾ ዓጸዎ) and represents a common translation from Tigrinya error. Option D incorrectly places the verb before the subject without an auxiliary in a declarative statement.
questions.tip: Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

options.B: They are very proud of their exam results.
options.C: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.
options.D: We were delighted to receive your letter.

why: Answer C: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.
Look at each sentence: is there a verb between the subject and the words that describe it?
A (is), B (are) and D (were) all have a linking verb.
C has no verb: *My brother ___ a hardworking farmer.* Correct: *My brother **is** a hardworking farmer.*
Tigrinya speakers sometimes leave out "is" because it can be dropped in Tigrinya. English always needs it.

Complete the sentence with the correct word order:

options.A: The rain was heavy, we decided to stay indoors.
options.B: The rain was heavy we decided to stay indoors.
options.C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.
options.D: Because the rain was heavy, so we decided to stay indoors.

why: Answer C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.

A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined with only a comma. Option A is a comma splice. Option B is a run-on sentence. Option C uses a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb ('therefore'), which is structurally perfect.

Option D is a double-conjunction error ('Because... so...'). Tigrinya speakers often use both because they translate word endings like "ስለዝ-... ስለዚ..." directly into English. Option C correctly separates the clauses.

Which of the following ditransitive sentences is g

options.A: yesterday welcomed the new students warmly
options.B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday
options.C: welcomed yesterday warmly the new students
options.D: the new students welcomed warmly yesterday

why: Answer B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday

English adverbs of manner ('warmly') usually precede the main verb or follow the object. Adverbs of time ('yesterday') belong at the end of the sentence. The correct structure is: Subject ('The school principal') + Adverb of Manner ('warmly') + Verb ('welcomed') + Object ('the new students') + Adverb of Time ('yesterday').

Option D shows S-O-V word order. Option A places the time adverb ('yesterday') between the subject and the verb, which is acceptable in Tigrinya but highly irregular and awkward in English unless formatted as a fronted adverbial.

Identify the sentence that has a word order error

options.A: The grandmother told a beautiful story her grandchildren.
options.B: The grandmother told to her grandchildren a beautiful story.
options.C: The grandmother told her grandchildren a beautiful story.
options.D: The grandmother her grandchildren a beautiful story told.

why: Answer C: The grandmother told her grandchildren a beautiful story.
Ditransitive verbs ('tell', 'give', 'buy') can take two structures: S + V + Indirect Object (IO) + Direct Object (DO) OR S + V + DO + to/for + IO.
Option C follows the S-V-IO-DO pattern ('her grandchildren' is IO, 'a beautiful story' is DO). Option A lacks the preposition 'to' which is required if DO comes before IO. Option D is an S-O-V trap.
questions.tip: Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

questions.label: 6. Identify the sentence that has a word order error due to the

options.A: He is not a member of the organizing committee.
options.B: They are not ready to take the national examination.
options.C: She is a doctor not in this public hospital.
options.D: We are not satisfied with the current classroom conditions.

why: Answer C: She is a doctor not in this public hospital.
With a linking verb, *not* comes straight after it: Subject + is/are + **not** + the rest.
*She is **not** a doctor in this public hospital.*
In C, *not* is in the wrong place (after *a doctor*).

options.A: Although the storm damaged many homes, the community rebuilt quickly.
options.B: The storm damaged many homes, but the community rebuilt quickly.
options.C: The storm damaged many homes the community rebuilt quickly.
options.D: The storm damaged many homes; the community rebuilt quickly.

why: Answer C: The storm damaged many homes the community rebuilt quickly.
A run-on sentence occurs when two independent clauses are joined without any punctuation or coordinating conjunctions.

Option C strings 'The storm damaged many homes' and 'the community rebuilt quickly' together with zero punctuation. Tigrinya speakers, used to inflectional markers on verbs for clausal relationships, often overlook the strict English requirement for punctuation boundaries or conjunctions.

similar.q: Identify the sentence that contains a linking verb

options.A: The athlete ran in the stadium gracefully this morning.
options.B: The athlete ran gracefully this morning in the stadium.
options.C: The athlete ran gracefully in the stadium this morning.
options.D: This morning the athlete ran in the stadium gracefully.

why: Answer C: The athlete ran gracefully in the stadium this morning.
When multiple adverbials modify a single verb, English follows the sequence: Manner (How) → Place (Where) → Time (When).

In Option C: 'gracefully' (Manner), 'in the stadium' (Place), and 'this morning' (Time) are correctly sequenced (M → P → T). Other options violate this standard order, which is a frequent target in matric grammar tasks.

similar.q: Choose the sentence that correctly manages sentenc

options.A: The adverb of time 'last week' is at the end.
options.B: There is a double subject ('My cousin' and 'he').
options.D: The direct object 'a new car' is misplaced.

why: Answer B: There is a double subject ('My cousin' and 'he').
In English, a noun subject must not be followed immediately by its corresponding pronoun subject in the same clause. This creates a redundant double subject.

In Tigrinya, verbs are conjugated with pronominal suffixes that match the subject (e.g., ወዲ ሓወይ መኪና ዓዲጉ - where the verb contains the subject marker). Direct translation often causes students to state the subject and then immediately repeat it with a pronoun ('My cousin he...').

options.A: Where you did buy that beautiful traditional dress?
options.B: Where did you buy that beautiful traditional dress?
options.C: Where you bought that beautiful traditional dress?
options.D: You bought that beautiful traditional dress where?

why: Answer B: Where did you buy that beautiful traditional dress?
English Wh-questions with active verbs require subject-auxiliary inversion: Wh-word + Auxiliary Verb (do/does/did) + Subject + Base Verb + Object.
Option B correctly inverts 'did' and 'you'. Option A and Option C are common translation from Tigrinya errors where the speaker maintains standard declarative word order (Wh-word + Subject + Verb).

similar.q: Identify: "He became a doctor." "a doctor" is ____.
Identify: "He saw a doctor." "a doctor" is ____.

why: Answer B: a subject complement
"is" is a linking verb.
What follows a linking verb and renames the subject is a subject complement.
It is not an object because "is" does not show action.
questions.tip: Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

units.title: Subject–verb agreement
units.intro: The verb must agree with its true subject in number, even when phrases come between them.

cards.title: Basic agreement
rule: Singular subject → singular verb: *The exam **starts** at eight.*
Plural subject → plural verb: *The exams **start** at eight.*
A phrase between subject and verb does not change agreement: *The box of books **is** heavy.*

examples.text: The list of names is long.
The list of names are long.
examples.fix: The list of names is long.

cards.title: Finding the real subject
body: The verb must agree with the **head noun** of the subject, which is often far from the verb. Cross out phrases that come between them: *The box ✗ *of oranges* **is** heavy; The students ✗ *in the last row* **are** quiet.*
Relative clauses do the same: *The man ✗ *who sells vegetables* **lives** next door.*
In present simple, a singular third-person subject (he, she, it, one person or thing) takes **-s**: *The bus **leaves** at seven.* Plural subjects take the base form: *The buses **leave** at seven.*
Two subjects joined by **and** are plural: *Aster and Ruth **are** cousins* – except when they form one idea: *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The list of names are long."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Singular subject → singular verb: *The exam **starts** at eight.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The list of names are long." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The list of names is long."
**Check:** Plural subject → plural verb: *The exams **start** at eight.*

cards.answer: The list of names is long.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The box of pens ____ on the desk.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The head noun is "box" (singular).

**Step 2:** "of pens" is a prepositional phrase and does not change agreement.

**Step 3:** So: is.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My brother and my sister ____ at university.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Two subjects joined by "and" make a plural subject.

**Step 2:** So the verb is plural: are.

**Step 3:** "is" would agree with only one person.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1:** The head noun is "The girl" (singular).

**Step 2:** "who sells newspapers" is a relative clause between subject and verb.

**Step 3:** Present simple singular: lives.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

cards.title: Tricky cases
rule: *each / every / everybody* → singular.
*either … or / neither … nor* → agree with the nearer noun.
Collective nouns may be singular when the group acts as one.

examples.fix: Everybody wants to pass.

examples.text: Neither the teachers nor the principal was late.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Everybody want to pass."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** *each / every / everybody* → singular.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Everybody want to pass." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Everybody wants to pass."
**Check:** *either … or / neither … nor* → agree with the nearer noun.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Ignore prepositional phrases after the subject; agree with the head noun.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Singular subjects take singular verbs; plural subjects take plural verbs; watch collective and either/or.

cards.title: Step by step: Tricky cases of subject–verb agreement
body: **Step 1:** Find the real subject (the head noun) and ignore phrases between it and the verb: "The box of pens IS on the desk."
**Step 2:** Words joined by "and" are plural: "Ali and Sara ARE here." – but "each/every + noun and noun" is singular.
**Step 3:** "Either…or / neither…nor / or / not only…but also": the verb agrees with the nearer subject: "Neither the teacher nor the students WERE late."
**Step 4:** Indefinite pronouns everyone, somebody, nobody, each, either, neither take a singular verb; both, few, many, several take a plural verb.
**Step 5:** Collective nouns (team, family, government) are usually singular when acting as one unit; amounts of money, time and distance are singular: "Ten kilometres IS a long walk."
**Example:** "The quality of the mangoes (is/are) good." Head noun = quality (singular) → "is". "Neither the coach nor the players (was/were) ready." Nearer subject = players → "were".

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Cross out, then count"
body: cross out the phrase after the head noun, then count the subject that is left (one = -s verb).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: In exam sentences, the noun just before the verb is often a trap ("of the students"). Always trace the verb back to the word that does the action.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Neither of your classmates ______ to come for the English General Knowledge.
cards.why: When 'Neither of' is followed by a plural noun, the verb is traditionally singular ('wants') because it refers to 'not one' of the group.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Each of the players ____ a new shirt.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "Each" is singular even when followed by "of + plural".

**Step 2:** So the verb is singular: has.

**Step 3:** "of the players" does not change agreement.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Either the students or the teacher ____ going to present.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** With either ... or, agree with the nearer subject.

**Step 2:** The nearer subject is "the teacher" (singular).

**Step 3:** So: is.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

units.title: Modals & semi-modals
units.intro: Modals (*can, must, should, might…*) express ability, obligation, advice and possibility without *to*.

cards.title: Core modals
rule: **must** = obligation that comes from the **speaker** (*I must study harder*); **have to** = obligation from **outside** – a rule, law or timetable (*We have to wear a uniform*); **should / ought to** = advice.
**can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.
Modal + bare infinitive: *You should revise.*

examples.fix: You should revise tonight.

cards.title: Choosing a modal by meaning
body: Modals add attitude to a verb. Always ask *what is the speaker's meaning?* – **obligation** (must, have to), **no obligation** (don't have to, needn't), **prohibition** (mustn't), **advice** (should, ought to), **ability** (can, could), **permission** (can, may), **possibility** (may, might, could).
**must** usually shows the speaker's own feeling or a rule; **have to** often shows an outside rule: *I must study tonight* vs *We have to wear uniform.* In the past both become **had to**.
Grammar of modals: no -s (*she can*), no to (*you should go*), questions by inversion (*Can you help?*), negatives with not (*mustn't, can't*).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "You should to revise tonight."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **must / have to** = obligation; **should / ought to** = advice.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "You should to revise tonight." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "You should revise tonight."
**Check:** **can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Modal
Use
rows: strong obligation from the speaker (I feel it is necessary)
obligation from outside: rule, law, timetable

cards.title: Must vs have to: the difference in one table
head: Point
must
have to
rows: the speaker: *I must call my mother tonight.*
outside (law, school, doctor, timetable): *Drivers have to carry a licence.*
*Passengers must wear seat belts.* (the rule-maker speaking)
**don't have to** = not necessary: *You don't have to pay; it's free.*
don't have to = needn't = there is no need
**had to**: *We had to wait for two hours.*
**will have to**: *You will have to apply online.*
*Do I have to…? Does she have to…? Did they have to…?*
**have got to** = have to: *I've got to go now.*

cards.title: Step by step: choose the right form
cards.problem: Complete: (a) The school rule says students ____ be in class by 7:30. (b) This film is wonderful – you ____ see it! (c) You ____ use your phone during the exam. (d) It's a holiday tomorrow, so we ____ go to school. (e) Last night I ____ finish my project, so I went to bed late.

steps.text: **Step 1: Is it necessary, forbidden or not necessary?** (a) necessary (b) necessary (c) forbidden (d) not necessary (e) necessary.
**Step 2: Necessary – who decides?** (a) the school → **have to**. (b) the speaker's own strong feeling → **must**.
**Step 3: Forbidden → mustn't.** (c) You **mustn't** use your phone.
**Step 4: Not necessary → don't have to (or needn't).** (d) we **don't have to** go to school.
**Step 5: Past → had to.** (e) Last night I **had to** finish my project.

cards.answer: (a) have to (b) must (c) mustn't (d) don't have to (e) had to

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In many countries, citizens ____ pay tax on what they earn. It is the law.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The obligation comes from outside: the law.

**Step 2:** Present time → **have to**.

**Step 3:** *mustn't* = forbidden; *don't have to* = not necessary – both change the meaning.

**Tip:** Necessary because I say so → must. Necessary because of a rule/law/timetable → have to. Forbidden → mustn't. Not necessary → don't have to / needn't. Past → had to.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: You ____ come to the airport with me. I can take a taxi.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "I can take a taxi" shows coming is **not necessary**.

**Step 2:** Not necessary → **don't have to** (or *needn't*).

**Step 3:** *mustn't* would mean you are not allowed to come.

**Tip:** Necessary because I say so → must. Necessary because of a rule/law/timetable → have to. Forbidden → mustn't. Not necessary → don't have to / needn't. Past → had to.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When the bridge was broken, the villagers ____ cross the river by boat.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *was broken* → past time.

**Step 2:** Past obligation = **had to** (*must* has no past form).

**Step 3:** *must have* + V3 is a guess about the past, not an obligation.

**Tip:** Necessary because I say so → must. Necessary because of a rule/law/timetable → have to. Forbidden → mustn't. Not necessary → don't have to / needn't. Past → had to.

cards.title: Step by step: Core modals
body: **Step 1:** Modals (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive: "She must go" (not "must to go" or "must goes").
**Step 2:** Choose by meaning: ability (can, could), permission (can, may, could), possibility (may, might, could), obligation (must, have to), advice (should, ought to), prohibition (mustn't).
**Step 3:** "Mustn't" = it is forbidden; "don't have to / needn't" = it is not necessary.
**Step 4:** Past forms: could (past ability), had to (past obligation); speculation about the past uses modal + have + V3: "He must have left."
**Step 5:** Modals never take -s and form questions/negatives without "do": "Can you swim?", "You should not shout."

**Example:** "You ___ wear a uniform; it's optional." → "don't have to" (no obligation). "You ___ smoke in the laboratory." → "mustn't" (prohibition). "She ___ have taken the bus; her car is here." → "must" (logical certainty about the past).

**Step 3:** Choice D uses "Perhaps" (ምናልባት), which is the correct synonym for 'might'.

cards.title: Perfect modals
rule: **must have + V3** = logical conclusion about the past.
**should have + V3** = past advice / regret.
**could have + V3** = past possibility that did not happen.

examples.fix: She must have left early.

cards.title: Perfect modals in context
body: Perfect modals look back at the past: **modal + have + past participle**.
**must have** = I'm sure it happened (*The streets are wet – it must have rained*). **can't/couldn't have** = I'm sure it didn't happen. **may/might/could have** = perhaps it happened.
**should have** = it was the right thing but it didn't happen (regret or criticism): *You should have revised.* **shouldn't have** = it happened, but it was wrong.
**could have** can also mean a chance that was not taken: *We could have won if we had trained.* **needn't have** = done, but unnecessary.

units.title: Active and passive voice
units.intro: Passive = be + past participle. Use it when the receiver matters more than the doer.

cards.title: Forming the passive
rule: Active S-V-O → Passive: object becomes subject + **be + V3** (+ by-agent).
Tense of be matches the active tense: writes→is written; wrote→was written.
Do not omit be: *The bridge was built*, not *The bridge built*.

examples.fix: The report was written yesterday.

examples.text: The gate is locked every night.

cards.title: From active to passive in three steps
body: **Step 1:** Take the object of the active sentence and make it the new subject: *The students planted **the trees*** → ***The trees** ...*
**Step 2:** Put "be" in the same tense as the active verb and add the past participle: planted (past simple) → **were planted**.
**Step 3:** Add *by + agent* only if it is important: *The trees were planted (by the students).*
Typical first-language (Tigrinya) trap: Tigrinya passives are formed on the verb itself (*ተሰሪሑ*), so learners drop "be": ✗ *The school built in 1990* → **The school was built in 1990**.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The report written yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Active S-V-O → Passive: object becomes subject + **be + V3** (+ by-agent).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The report written yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The report was written yesterday."
**Check:** Tense of be matches the active tense: writes→is written; wrote→was written.

cards.title: Step by step: Forming the passive
body: **Step 1:** Take the object of the active sentence and make it the subject: "Workers built the bridge" → "The bridge…".
**Step 2:** Put "be" in the same tense as the active verb (built = past simple → was/were).
**Step 3:** Add the past participle (V3) of the main verb: "The bridge was built".
**Step 4:** Add "by + agent" only if the doer is important or new information: "…by Italian engineers."
**Step 5:** Only transitive verbs (verbs with an object) can become passive: "arrive, happen, die" have no passive.
**Example:** Active: "The government opened a new school in Keren." → Passive: "A new school was opened in Keren (by the government)." Present: "They grow coffee here." → "Coffee is grown here."

cards.title: Mnemonic — "O-B-3"
body: Object first, Be in the same tense, V3 last.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Check the tense of "be" against the active verb – most mistakes are tense mismatches ("is built" for a past action).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The World Cup 2022 matches were being televised all over the world. (Choose the correct active form)

options.A: All over the world, the World Cup 2022 matches were being televised.
options.B: Television channels televised the World Cup 2022 matches all over the world.
options.C: Television channels were televising the World Cup 2022 matches all over the world.
options.D: All over the world, the World Cup 2022 football matches were televised.
options.E: The World Cup 2022 matches televised all over the world.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify the tense. "Were being televised" is **Past Continuous Passive**.
**Step 2:** The active form must also be in Past Continuous (**was/were + verb-ing**).
**Step 3:** "Television channels were televising" is the correct active conversion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Which of the following is the **passive voice form** of the sentence in italics?

*My mother advised me not to go out alone.*

options.A: I am advised not to go out alone.
options.B: I had been advised not to go out alone.
options.C: I advised my mother not to out alone.
options.D: I was advised not to go out alone.
options.E: I always advise not to go out alone.

cards.why: The active sentence is in the Past Simple ('advised'). To convert to passive, 'me' becomes 'I', and we use 'was/were + V3'. Thus, 'I was advised' is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the passive form of "The workers repaired the road."

options.A: The workers were repaired by the road.
options.B: The road was repair by the workers.
options.C: The road was repaired by the workers.
options.D: The road repaired by the workers.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The object "the road" becomes the subject.

**Step 2:** Past simple active → was + V3 (repaired).

**Step 3:** Option B drops "be"; C lacks -ed; D reverses the meaning.

**Tip:** Passive = correct tense of "be" + past participle (V3). Keep the tense of the active verb in the form of "be", and never drop "be".

cards.title: Progressive and perfect passives
rule: Progressive: *is being cleaned*.
Perfect: *has been signed*.
Future: *will be completed* / *will have been completed*.

examples.fix: The room is being painted. / has been painted.

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Progressive: *is being cleaned*.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The room is been painted." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The room is being painted. / has been painted."
**Check:** Perfect: *has been signed*.

cards.answer: The room is being painted. / has been painted.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: If the subject is inanimate and cannot perform the action, expect a passive.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Form passives with the correct be-tense + V3; do not drop be (first-language (Tigrinya) trap).

cards.title: Step by step: Progressive and perfect passives
body: **Step 1:** Progressive passive = be (am/is/are/was/were) + being + V3: "The road is being repaired now."
**Step 2:** Perfect passive = have/has/had + been + V3: "The letters have been sent."
**Step 3:** Future and modal passives = will/can/must + be + V3: "The results will be announced tomorrow."
**Step 4:** Find the tense of the active verb first, then keep the same tense in the passive auxiliary.
**Step 5:** Never drop "be/been/being": "The letter sent" is wrong; "The letter was sent" is right.

**Example:** Active: "They are building a new hospital." → "A new hospital is being built." Active: "Someone has stolen my bag." → "My bag has been stolen." Active: "They had finished the work." → "The work had been finished."

cards.title: Mnemonic — "-ing tense → BEING, perfect tense → BEEN"
body: the passive marker copies the active tense.

cards.title: Exam tip

options.C: Mr. Munir’s office have been painted.

**Step 1:** Identify the tense. 'is painting' is Present Continuous.
**Step 2:** The passive structure for Present Continuous is 'am/is/are + being + V3'.
**Step 3:** 'Mr. Munir's office' is singular, so we use 'is being painted'.
**Result:** Option A.

units.title: Reported speech
units.intro: Reported speech shifts tense and pronouns when the reporting verb is past.

cards.title: Backshift basics
rule: Direct: *“I am ready,” she said.* → Reported: *She said (that) she was ready.*
will → would; can → could; have done → had done.
*tell* needs a person object: *He told me to wait.*

examples.text: She said she is tired yesterday.
examples.fix: She said she was tired.

cards.title: The backshift table
body: When the reporting verb is past (*said, told, asked*), move each tense one step back: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect / past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to.
Change time and place words: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the day before; here → there; this → that; ago → before.
No backshift is needed when the fact is still true or the reporting verb is present: *She says she **is** tired; He said the Earth **goes** round the sun.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She said she is tired yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Direct: *“I am ready,” she said.* → Reported: *She said (that) she was ready.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She said she is tired yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She said she was tired."
**Check:** will → would; can → could; have done → had done.

Reported

"**We** love **our** school." → They said **they** loved **their** school.
He said to me, "**You** are late." → He told me **I** was late.
he, she, they / his, her, their
I said to Abel, "**Your** bag is here." → I told Abel **his** bag was there.

head: Type
Reporting verb + pattern
Direct
Reported

She asked me **to close** the door.
The teacher told us **to sit** down.

cards.title: When the tense does NOT change
body: 1. The reporting verb is in the **present** (*says, has said, will say*): *"I am hungry."* → *She **says** she **is** hungry.*
2. The words are a **general truth** or still true: *"Water boils at 100 °C."* → *The teacher said water **boils** at 100 °C.*
3. The verb is already **past perfect**, or a modal like **would, could, should, might, ought to**.
**say or tell?** *say* has no person after it (*She said that…*, *She said to me…*). *tell* always has a person (*She **told me** that…*). ✗ *She said me*. ✗ *She told that*.

cards.title: Step by step: report a statement
cards.problem: Report: Hana said to me, "I am going to visit my aunt in Keren tomorrow."

steps.text: **Step 1: Reporting verb.** *said to me* → **told me** (tell + person).
**Step 2: Pronouns.** *I* → **she**; *my* → **her** (Hana is a woman).
**Step 3: Tense one step back.** *am going to* → **was going to**.
**Step 4: Time and place words.** *tomorrow* → **the next day**. (*Keren* is a name – no change.)
**Step 5: Put it together.** Hana told me (that) she was going to visit her aunt in Keren the next day.

cards.answer: Hana told me (that) she was going to visit her aunt in Keren the next day.

cards.title: Step by step: report a question
cards.problem: Report: He asked me, "Where did you buy this book yesterday?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Keep the question word.** *where*.
**Step 2: Statement order, no did.** *did you buy* → *you bought*.
**Step 3: Pronoun.** *you* (= me) → **I**.
**Step 4: Tense back.** past simple *bought* → past perfect **had bought**.
**Step 5: Time/place words.** *this* → **that**; *yesterday* → **the day before**.
**Step 6: Full stop, not a question mark.** He asked me where I had bought that book the day before.

cards.answer: He asked me where I had bought that book the day before.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Selam said, "I have finished my homework." → Selam said that she ____ her homework.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *said* is past, so move the tense one step back.

**Step 2:** present perfect (*have finished*) → past perfect (**had finished**).

**Step 3:** *my* → *her* is already done in the sentence.

**Tip:** Change in this order: (1) reporting verb, (2) pronouns, (3) tense one step back, (4) time and place words, (5) word order for questions.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The teacher said to us, "Don't open your books." → The teacher told us ____ our books.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** It is a negative command.

**Step 2:** Pattern: told + person + **not to** + verb.

**Step 3:** So: *The teacher told us not to open our books.*

**Tip:** Change in this order: (1) reporting verb, (2) pronouns, (3) tense one step back, (4) time and place words, (5) word order for questions.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He asked me, "Can you help me tomorrow?" → He asked me ____.

options.A: if I could help him the next day
options.C: if could I help him the next day
options.D: that I could help him tomorrow

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Yes/no question → **if / whether**.

**Step 2:** Statement order: *I could* (can → could).

**Step 3:** Pronouns: you → I, me → him. Time: tomorrow → the next day.

**Tip:** Change in this order: (1) reporting verb, (2) pronouns, (3) tense one step back, (4) time and place words, (5) word order for questions.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "I will call you tonight," Dawit said to Ruth. → Dawit told Ruth that he ____ her that night.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *will* moves back to **would**.

**Step 2:** *you* (Ruth) → *her*; *tonight* → *that night* (already in the sentence).

**Step 3:** So: *Dawit told Ruth that he would call her that night.*

**Tip:** Change in this order: (1) reporting verb, (2) pronouns, (3) tense one step back, (4) time and place words, (5) word order for questions.

cards.title: Step by step: Backshift in reported speech
body: **Step 1:** When the reporting verb is past (said, told, asked), move each tense one step back.
**Step 2:** present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect / past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might.
**Step 3:** Change pronouns to fit the new speaker: "I" → he/she, "my" → his/her.
**Step 4:** Change time and place words: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there.
**Step 5:** Questions become statement order with if/whether or the wh-word; commands become told/asked + (not) to + verb.

**Example:** Direct: Saba said, "I am studying for my exam tomorrow." → Reported: Saba said (that) she was studying for her exam the next day. Direct: He asked, "Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Tense back, Person shift, Time and place change"
body: T-P-T.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Do all three changes in order: tense, then pronoun, then time/place word. Examiners mark each change separately.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He said, ”I had seen the film before.”

options.A: He said that he has seen the film by now.
options.B: He said that he has seen the film before.
options.C: He said that he had seen the film before.
options.D: He ordered that to see the film.

cards.why: When the direct speech is already in the Past Perfect ('had seen'), it remains in the Past Perfect in indirect speech. Note: Option B uses 'has seen' (Present Perfect), which is incorrect. Option C is the correct conversion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He said that he had to go at once.

options.A: The boy said, ”I will have to go at once.”
options.B: The boy said, ”I must to go at once.”
options.C: The boy said, ”I have to go at once.”
options.D: The boy said, ”I had to go at once.”
options.E: The boy said, ”I want to go at once.”

cards.why: When converting indirect speech with 'had to' back to direct speech, 'had to' usually changes back to 'have to' or 'must'. Option B is grammatically incorrect ('must to' is wrong). Therefore, 'I have to go at once' is the correct direct form.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: They said that they were going to church. (Change to Direct Speech)

options.A: They said, “They were going to church.”
options.B: They said, “We were going to church.”
options.C: They said, “We are going to church.”
options.D: They said, “They are going to church

cards.why: To change from indirect to direct speech: the past continuous 'were going' changes back to present continuous 'are going', and the pronoun 'they' (referring to the speakers) changes to 'we'.

cards.title: Questions and commands
rule: Yes/No: *asked if/whether* + clause (no do/does/did).
Wh-questions: keep the wh-word; use statement order.
Commands: *told/asked + object + to-infinitive*.

examples.text: She asked if I was ready.

examples.fix: She asked if I was ready.

examples.text: He told us to sit down.

cards.title: Reporting questions and commands
body: **Yes/no questions:** asked + if/whether + statement order: *"Are you hungry?" → She asked if I was hungry.*
**Wh-questions:** keep the wh-word, use statement order and no do/does/did: *"Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.*
**Commands and requests:** tell/ask/order + person + (not) to-infinitive: *"Close the door." → She told me to close the door. "Don't shout." → He asked us not to shout.*
Other useful reporting verbs: advise, remind, warn, invite, refuse, promise – each with its own pattern (*He promised to come; She warned me not to touch it*).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She asked was I ready."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Yes/No: *asked if/whether* + clause (no do/does/did).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She asked was I ready." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She asked if I was ready."
**Check:** Wh-questions: keep the wh-word; use statement order.

cards.answer: She asked if I was ready.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Backshift: present→past, past→past perfect, will→would; keep place/time words consistent.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Use told + person, said (that)…; adjust tense when the reporting verb is past.

units.title: Conditionals & wish
units.intro: Match if-clause and result tenses: 0/1 real, 2 unreal present, 3 unreal past, mixed for past→present.

cards.title: Types 0–3
rule: 0: If + present, present (facts).
1: If + present, will + V (real future).
2: If + past, would + V (unreal now); prefer *were*.
3: If + past perfect, would have + V3 (unreal past).

examples.text: If it rains, we will stay in.
If it will rain, we will stay in.
examples.fix: If it rains, we will stay in.

examples.text: If I were you, I would apply.

cards.title: Choosing the right conditional
body: Ask two questions: **Is it real or unreal?** and **Is it about the present/future or the past?**
**Real, always true → Type 0:** *If you press this, the light comes on.* **Real, possible future → Type 1:** *If it rains, we'll stay in.*
**Unreal present/future → Type 2:** *If I had wings, I would fly* (I don't have wings). **Unreal past → Type 3:** *If she had trained, she would have won* (she didn't train).
The if-clause can come second without a comma: *We'll stay in if it rains.* "Unless" = if not; "provided / as long as" = only if.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "If it will rain, we will stay in."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** 0: If + present, present (facts).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "If it will rain, we will stay in." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "If it rains, we will stay in."
**Check:** 1: If + present, will + V (real future).

cards.answer: If it rains, we will stay in.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Type
Form
rows: If + had + V3, would have + V3

cards.title: Step by step: Conditional types 0–3
body: **Step 1:** Type 0 (always true facts): If + present simple, present simple – "If you heat ice, it melts."
**Step 2:** Type 1 (real/possible future): If + present simple, will + verb – "If it rains, we will stay home."
**Step 3:** Type 2 (unreal or unlikely present/future): If + past simple, would + verb – "If I had wings, I would fly." (use "were" for all persons: If I were you…).
**Step 4:** Type 3 (unreal past, regret): If + had + V3, would have + V3 – "If he had studied, he would have passed."
**Step 5:** Never put "will" or "would" in the if-clause; "unless" = if not.
**Example:** "If she ___ (know) your number, she would call you." → knew (Type 2). "If they had left earlier, they ___ (catch) the bus." → would have caught (Type 3).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "0 = fact, 1 = likely, 2 = dream, 3 = regret"
body: and the verb in the if-clause goes one step back each time (present → past → past perfect).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Identify the type from the tense already given in one clause, then build the other clause to match.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If you ____ ice, it melts.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** This is a general fact: type 0.

**Step 2:** Type 0 uses the present simple in both clauses.

**Step 3:** So: If you heat ice, it melts.

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If I ____ the answer, I would tell you.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "would tell" shows an unreal present situation: type 2.

**Step 2:** The if-clause takes the past simple.

**Step 3:** So: If I knew the answer ...

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If she had asked me, I ____ her.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "had asked" shows type 3 (unreal past).

**Step 2:** The main clause takes would have + past participle.

**Step 3:** So: I would have helped her.

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Mixed conditionals and wish
rule: Past cause → present result: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*
Wish + past = present regret; wish + past perfect = past regret.
Inverted forms: *Had I known…*, *Were I you…*, *Should you need…*.

examples.text: If she had trained, she would be fitter now.
I wish I had prepared yesterday.

examples.fix: I wish I had prepared yesterday.

cards.title: Expressing wishes and regrets
body: **wish + past simple** = I want the present to be different: *I wish I **had** more time* (I don't have enough).
**wish + past perfect** = regret about the past: *I wish I **had studied** harder* (I didn't).
**wish + would** = complaint about someone's behaviour: *I wish you **would** stop talking.*
"If only" is a stronger form of wish: *If only I had listened!*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "I wish I prepared yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Past cause → present result: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "I wish I prepared yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "I wish I had prepared yesterday."
**Check:** Wish + past = present regret; wish + past perfect = past regret.

cards.answer: I wish I had prepared yesterday.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Never put would in the if-clause of type 2/3; use were for formal type 2.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Zero/first for facts and real futures; second/third for unreal present/past; wish uses unreal past forms.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I wish I knew Ali's mobile phone number.

options.C: I don't know the number and I regret this.

cards.why:
**Analysis:** The structure "I wish + Past Simple" is used to express a regret about a present situation. It means the opposite of the current reality. 
**Reality:** I **do not know** the number right now, and I am unhappy about it. Choice C correctly captures both the fact and the feeling.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If they had waited another month, they could probably __________ a better price for their house.
cards.why: This is a **Third Conditional** sentence (unreal past). The structure is: If + Past Perfect, Subject + could/would + have + Past Participle. Therefore, 'have got' is the correct completion.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
The sentence describes two actions in the past: preparing everything and leaving. When one past action happens before another past action, we use the **Past Perfect Tense** (had + past participle) for the earlier action. 

1. First Action: Preparing (Past Perfect)
2. Second Action: Leaving (Simple Past)

units.title: Gerunds, infinitives & participles
units.intro: Some verbs take -ing, some take to-infinitive; prepositions take -ing.

cards.title: Verb patterns
rule: enjoy/avoid/suggest/finish + -ing.
want/decide/hope/plan + to-infinitive.
stop + -ing = quit; stop + to-V = pause in order to.

examples.fix: She enjoys reading.

cards.title: Common verb patterns to memorise
body: **Verb + -ing:** enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, keep, practise, deny, admit, imagine, risk.
**Verb + to-infinitive:** want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse, promise, offer, manage, afford, learn, expect.
**Verb + object + to-infinitive:** ask, tell, advise, allow, encourage, warn (*She advised me to rest*). **Verb + object + bare infinitive:** let, make (*They made us wait*).
**Change of meaning:** remember/forget + -ing (past memory) vs + to (future duty); stop + -ing (quit) vs + to (in order to); try + -ing (experiment) vs + to (make an effort).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She enjoys to read."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** enjoy/avoid/suggest/finish + -ing.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She enjoys to read." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She enjoys reading."
**Check:** want/decide/hope/plan + to-infinitive.

cards.title: Step by step: Verb patterns
body: **Step 1:** Some verbs are followed by -ing (gerund): enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, keep, practise, deny, admit, imagine, risk.
**Step 2:** Some verbs are followed by to-infinitive: want, decide, hope, plan, agree, promise, refuse, offer, expect, manage, learn.
**Step 3:** Some take object + to-infinitive: ask, tell, advise, allow, encourage, warn, want + someone + to do.

**Step 4:** Some change meaning: stop doing (quit) vs stop to do (stop in order to); remember doing (memory of the past) vs remember to do (not forget a duty); try doing (experiment) vs try to do (make an effort).
**Step 5:** "Make" and "let" take object + bare infinitive: "She made me wait."
**Example:** "He avoided ___ (answer) the question." → answering. "They decided ___ (build) a school." → to build. "I stopped ___ (buy) bread on the way home." → to buy (stopped in order to buy).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Enjoy-Avoid-Finish = -ING" (E.A.F.) and "Want-Decide-Hope = TO" (W.D.H.).
body: "Enjoy-Avoid-Finish = -ING" (E.A.F.) and "Want-Decide-Hope = TO" (W.D.H.).

cards.title: Exam tip
body: For stop/remember/try, decide the time order: if the action happened before → -ing; if it comes after (a purpose or duty) → to.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She said that the letter was personal and wouldn’t let me _____ it.
cards.why: The verb 'let' is followed by an object and then the bare infinitive (verb without 'to').

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "finish" is followed by a gerund (-ing).

**Step 2:** So: finished writing.

**Step 3:** "to write" is wrong after finish.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "forget + to-infinitive" refers to an action you need to do in the future.

**Step 2:** "forget + -ing" refers to a past memory.

**Step 3:** Here the action is in the future: to switch off.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

cards.title: Adjective + infinitive; preposition + -ing
rule: easy/hard/important + to-infinitive.
good at / interested in / before + -ing.
look forward to + -ing (*to* is a preposition here).

examples.text: She is interested in studying history.
I look forward to meet you.
examples.fix: I look forward to meeting you.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "I look forward to meet you."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** easy/hard/important + to-infinitive.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "I look forward to meet you." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "I look forward to meeting you."
**Check:** good at / interested in / before + -ing.

cards.answer: I look forward to meeting you.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: After a preposition always use a gerund: interested in learning.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Memorise high-frequency patterns; stop + -ing ≠ stop + to-infinitive.

cards.title: Step by step: Adjective + infinitive; preposition + -ing
body: **Step 1:** Many adjectives describing feelings or judgement take to-infinitive: happy to help, easy to learn, difficult to understand, ready to go, sorry to hear.
**Step 2:** Pattern "It is + adjective + (for someone) + to-infinitive": "It is important for students to read daily."
**Step 3:** After any preposition (in, on, at, of, about, for, without, before, after) the verb takes -ing: "interested in studying", "good at drawing", "without saying".
**Step 4:** Some phrases end in the preposition "to", so they also take -ing: look forward to meeting, be used to working, object to paying.
**Step 5:** "Too + adjective + to" and "adjective + enough + to": "too tired to walk", "old enough to vote".
**Example:** "She is afraid ___ (fly)." → of flying (preposition). "This question is easy ___ (answer)." → to answer. "I look forward to ___ (hear) from you." → hearing.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Preposition? Put -ING in position."
body: "Preposition? Put -ING in position."

cards.title: Exam tip
body: In letter endings the classic error is "look forward to hear". The "to" here is a preposition, so always write "look forward to hearing".

cards.why: The phrase 'be accustomed to' is followed by a gerund (-ing form). Here, 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

cards.why: The adjective 'interested' is always followed by the preposition **in** (e.g., interested in music, interested in sports).

**Step 1:** The fixed pattern is "afraid of + -ing / noun".

**Step 2:** After the preposition "of" the verb takes -ing.

**Step 3:** So: afraid of walking.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

units.title: Transitive & intransitive verbs; direct & indirect objects
units.intro: Textbook Unit 8 (Accidents) grammar: transitive verbs (with an object) and intransitive verbs (without an object), linking verbs with a complement, and verbs with two objects (direct and indirect).

cards.title: Transitive and intransitive verbs
rule: A **transitive verb** needs an **object**: a person or thing that receives the action. Ask *what?* or *whom?* after the verb: *He raised **his hands**.* (raised what? → his hands) *She told **a story**.*
An **intransitive verb** has **no object**. The sentence is complete without one: *The dog **barks**. The sun **rises** in the east.* (*in the east* tells us where; it is not an object.)
Many verbs can be **both**: *She **sings**.* (intransitive) / *She **sings** a song.* (transitive). *The door **opened**.* / *He **opened** the door.*

**Linking verbs** (*be, become, seem, look, go* = become, *fall* asleep, *prove, keep*) have no object, but they need a **complement** – a word that describes the subject: *The old man **went mad**. The child **has fallen asleep**. The information **proved false**.* (The textbook calls them *verbs of incomplete predication*.)
Only transitive verbs can be **passive**: *He told a story.* → *A story was told.* ✗ *An accident was happened.*

Watch these pairs: **raise** (+ object: *raise your hand*) / **rise** (no object: *prices rise*); **lay** (+ object: *lay the table*) / **lie** (no object: *lie down*). **arrive** has no object: *arrive **at** school* (✗ *arrive school*). **discuss** has an object: *discuss the plan* (✗ *discuss about*).

examples.fix: We discussed the accident.

cards.problem: Decide for each verb: (a) The children laughed loudly. (b) The children found a wallet. (c) The baby fell asleep. (d) We waited for the bus.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the verb.** (a) laughed (b) found (c) fell (d) waited.

**Step 2: Ask "what?" or "whom?" straight after the verb.** (a) laughed what? – nothing (*loudly* tells how). (b) found what? – **a wallet**. (c) fell what? – nothing, but *asleep* describes the baby. (d) waited what? – nothing (*for the bus* is a phrase with a preposition).
**Step 3: Decide.** (a) intransitive. (b) transitive, object = *a wallet*. (c) linking verb, complement = *asleep*. (d) intransitive.
**Check with the passive:** *A wallet was found by the children.* ✔ (transitive) – ✗ *The children were laughed.* (intransitive)

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Ask: slept what? – nothing.

**Step 2:** *peacefully* only tells us how. There is no object → **intransitive**.

**Step 3:** It is not linking: *peacefully* does not describe the man, it describes the sleeping.

**Tip:** Ask "what?" or "whom?" straight after the verb. A noun that receives the action = object → transitive. Nothing, or only how/where/when → intransitive. An adjective describing the subject → linking verb + complement.

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1:** There is no object after the gap → we need the intransitive verb **rise**.

**Step 2:** After *has* use the past participle: rise – rose – **risen**.

**Step 3:** *raised* needs an object (*raised the price*).

**Tip:** Ask "what?" or "whom?" straight after the verb. A noun that receives the action = object → transitive. Nothing, or only how/where/when → intransitive. An adjective describing the subject → linking verb + complement.

cards.title: Quick check

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Only verbs with an object can be passive.

**Step 2:** *arrived* has no object (intransitive) → no passive.

**Step 3:** A, B and D can be passive: *A letter was written. A bridge was built. The bus was stopped.*

**Tip:** Ask "what?" or "whom?" straight after the verb. A noun that receives the action = object → transitive. Nothing, or only how/where/when → intransitive. An adjective describing the subject → linking verb + complement.

cards.title: Direct and indirect objects
rule: Some verbs (**give, send, show, tell, bring, buy, lend, pass, write, read, offer, teach, make, promise**) can have **two objects**: *She gave **me** **a book**.*
The **direct object (DO)** is the **thing**: *a book* (ask *what?*). The **indirect object (IO)** is the **person** who receives it or gets the help: *me* (ask *to whom? / for whom?*).
Two patterns, same meaning: (1) **V + IO + DO**: *He wrote **Dan** **a letter**.* (2) **V + DO + to/for + IO**: *He wrote **a letter** **to Dan**.*

**to** = the person receives it (*give, send, show, tell, lend, pass, write, read, offer, teach, promise, sell*). **for** = we do it to help the person (*buy, make, get, cook, find, build, bring*): *I bought **her** a coffee.* = *I bought a coffee **for her**.*
When the direct object is a **pronoun** (*it, them*), use pattern 2: *Give **it to me**.* (✗ *Give me it* in exams.)
Some verbs use **only pattern 2**: **explain, describe, say, suggest, report, introduce**: *Explain **the rule to me*** (✗ *Explain me the rule*).

cards.title: Step by step: Textbook Lesson 8.8 A – correct the sentences
cards.problem: Correct: (1) He wrote to Dan a letter. (2) They gave a lot of presents Simon. (3) Can you show it me? (4) I have brought this book your sister.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the person (IO) and the thing (DO).** (1) Dan / a letter (2) Simon / presents (3) me / it (4) your sister / this book.
**Step 2: Choose a pattern.** Person first → no preposition. Thing first → add *to* or *for* before the person.
(1) He wrote **Dan a letter**. / He wrote **a letter to Dan**.
(2) They gave **Simon a lot of presents**. / They gave **a lot of presents to Simon**.
(3) *it* is a pronoun → pattern 2: Can you show **it to me**?
(4) *bring* to help someone → **for**: I have brought this book **for your sister**.

cards.answer: (1) He wrote Dan a letter. (2) They gave Simon a lot of presents. (3) Can you show it to me? (4) I have brought this book for your sister.

cards.title: Step by step: find the direct and the indirect object
cards.problem: She sent her grandmother a long letter.

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the verb.** *sent*.
**Step 2: Ask "sent what?"** → *a long letter* = **direct object** (the thing).
**Step 3: Ask "sent it to whom?"** → *her grandmother* = **indirect object** (the person).
**Step 4: Check with pattern 2.** *She sent a long letter **to** her grandmother.* ✔

cards.answer: Direct object: a long letter. Indirect object: her grandmother.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In 'The teacher gave us homework', the indirect object is ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** gave what? → *homework* (direct object).

**Step 2:** gave it to whom? → **us** (indirect object).

**Step 3:** *The teacher* is the subject.

**Tip:** Person + thing → V + person + thing (gave me a pen) or V + thing + to/for + person (gave a pen to me). If the thing is "it/them", use the second pattern.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correct sentence.

options.B: He explained the problem to me.
options.D: He explained for me the problem.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *explain* uses only pattern 2: explain + thing + **to** + person.

**Step 2:** So: *He explained the problem to me.*

**Step 3:** A is a very common mistake – *explain* cannot take the person straight after it.

**Tip:** Person + thing → V + person + thing (gave me a pen) or V + thing + to/for + person (gave a pen to me). If the thing is "it/them", use the second pattern.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I bought a new dress ____ my little sister.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *buy* = we do it to help the person → **for**.

**Step 2:** Pattern 1 is also possible: *I bought my little sister a new dress.*

**Step 3:** *to* is used with give, send, show, tell…

**Tip:** Person + thing → V + person + thing (gave me a pen) or V + thing + to/for + person (gave a pen to me). If the thing is "it/them", use the second pattern.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Please pass ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The direct object is the pronoun *it*.

**Step 2:** Pronoun object → pattern 2: pass **it to me**.

**Step 3:** A and B are avoided in standard written English; D has the wrong order.

**Tip:** Person + thing → V + person + thing (gave me a pen) or V + thing + to/for + person (gave a pen to me). If the thing is "it/them", use the second pattern.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Rewrite 'They gave a prize to the best student' with the indirect object first.

options.A: They gave the best student a prize.
options.B: They gave to the best student a prize.
options.C: They gave a prize the best student.
options.D: They the best student gave a prize.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Pattern 1 = V + person + thing, with **no** preposition.

**Step 2:** *They gave the best student a prize.*

**Step 3:** B keeps *to* (wrong in pattern 1); C drops *to* in pattern 2.

**Tip:** Person + thing → V + person + thing (gave me a pen) or V + thing + to/for + person (gave a pen to me). If the thing is "it/them", use the second pattern.

units.title: Nouns, Pluralization
units.intro: Nouns: countable, uncountable and plurals.

cards.title: Nouns: countable, uncountable and plurals
rule: **Countable nouns** can be counted: *a student, two students*. **Uncountable nouns** cannot: *information, advice, water, furniture, luggage, equipment, progress, homework, news*.
Uncountable nouns have **no plural** and no *a/an*: *some advice* (✗ advices), *a piece of advice, two items of luggage*. They take a **singular** verb: *The news **is** good.*
Use **many / a few / fewer** with countable nouns and **much / a little / less** with uncountable nouns: *many books, much time*.

Most plurals add **-s / -es / -ies**: *book → books, box → boxes, city → cities*. Learn the irregular ones: *man → men, child → children, tooth → teeth, criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena, crisis → crises*. Some stay the same: *sheep, deer, species, series*.
Abstract nouns used in general take **no article**: ***Honesty** is the best policy.* (✗ The honesty is…)

She gave me many useful advices.

cards.pattern: count: a/many/few + plural  ·  uncount: some/much/little + singular verb

cards.title: Notes
body: **In short:** ask "can I count it?" Yes → countable (a, many, few, plural). No → uncountable (much, little, a piece of, singular verb).
Words that are countable in Tigrinya but **uncountable** in English: *information, advice, news, furniture, luggage, equipment, homework, knowledge*.
Irregular plurals to learn: *child–children, foot–feet, mouse–mice, criterion–criteria, phenomenon–phenomena, crisis–crises, analysis–analyses*.

cards.title: Form tricky plurals
cards.problem: Write the plural of: box, baby, knife, child, sheep, potato, criterion.

steps.text: **Step 1: -s, -x, -ch, -sh, -z → add -es.** box → boxes.
**Step 2: consonant + y → -ies.** baby → babies.
**Step 3: many -f/-fe → -ves.** knife → knives.
**Step 4: irregular forms must be learnt.** child → children; sheep → sheep (no change).
**Step 5: some -o words take -es.** potato → potatoes.
**Step 6: Greek/Latin words.** criterion → criteria.
**Tip:** check the last letters first, then think of irregular and borrowed words.

cards.answer: boxes, babies, knives, children, sheep, potatoes, criteria.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The manager rejected the proposal because he felt that ________ details were provided to support the budget.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The blank modifies the noun 'details'. 'Details' is a plural countable noun (indicated by the '-s' ending).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Uncountable quantifiers like 'little' and 'a little' cannot modify plural countable nouns. 'Too few' is the correct quantifier for countable nouns in a negative context. Tigrinya speakers often conflate 'few' and 'little' as both translate to 'ውሑድ' or 'ቅሩብ'.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Details' (ዝርዝር ሓበሬታታት) ዝቝጸር ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (countable plural) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ምስኡ ክኸይድ ዝኽእል መለክዕ 'few' ጥራይ እዩ። 'Little' ንዘይቝጸሩ ስማት ጥራይ ስለ ዝገልጽ ክንጥቀመሉ ኣይንኽእልን። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'too few' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following sentences contains a pluralization error?

options.A: The laboratory analyzed various natural phenomena.
options.B: We must establish clear criteria for the scholarship.
options.C: The school board discussed several educational crisises.
options.D: The shepherd guided the sheep down the mountain.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Crisis' is a noun of Greek origin. Its plural form is 'crises', not 'crisises'.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
National exams frequently test irregular non-English plurals. Students often try to apply the regular '-es' rule to words ending in '-is' (like crisis, oasis, thesis), producing incorrect forms like 'crisises' (Option C).

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ናይ ግሪኽን ላቲንን መበቆል ዘለዎም ስማት ፍሉይ ናይ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ምስራዕ ኣለዎም። 'Crisis' (ቅልውላው) ዝብል ስም ኣብ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ክቕየር ከሎ 'crises' ይኸውን እምበር 'crisises' ኣይበሃልን። ስለዚ Option C ጌጋ ዘለዎ ምሉእ ሓሳብ እዩ።

units.title: Pronouns
units.intro: Grammar: subject, object, possessive and reflexive pronouns, and using it / its for things.

cards.title: Pronouns
rule: A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun so that we do not repeat it: *Aster is late. **She** missed the bus.*

**Subject pronouns** (*I, you, he, she, it, we, they*) come **before the verb**: ***She** writes.* **Object pronouns** (*me, you, him, her, it, us, them*) come **after a verb or a preposition**: *The teacher helped **her**. This letter is for **me**.*

**Possessive adjectives** (*my, your, his, her, its, our, their*) go **before a noun**: *the dog wagged **its** tail.* **Possessive pronouns** (*mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs*) stand **alone**: *The book is **mine**.* They never take an apostrophe: *its, hers, theirs* (*it's* = it is).
**Reflexive pronouns** (*myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves*) point back to the subject: *They did the work **themselves**.* (✗ *theirselves*, ✗ *hisself*)
Use **it / its** for things and animals, **he / she** for people: *The school opened **its** new library.*

**Two names joined by "and":** cover the other name and test the pronoun alone: *The teacher asked Ruth and (I / me)…* → *asked **me*** → *asked Ruth and **me***. *(I / Me) and Aster went…* → ***I** went* → *Aster and **I** went*.

examples.text: Aster and I went to the market.
The teacher gave the books to Ruth and me.

examples.fix: Aster and I went to the market.

head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: Me and my friend went home.

its = belonging to it; it's = it is

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My sister and ____ are going to Asmara next week.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The pronoun is part of the subject (before *are going*).

**Step 2:** Cover *My sister and*: *__ am going* → **I**.

**Step 3:** *me* is an object pronoun; *myself* needs *I* as the subject.

**Tip:** Before the verb → subject pronoun (I, he, she, we, they). After a verb or a preposition → object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them). Cover the other name and test.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The company has changed ____ name.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *company* is a thing (singular) → *it*.

**Step 2:** Before a noun (*name*) we need the possessive adjective **its**.

**Step 3:** *it's* means *it is* – "has changed it is name" makes no sense.

**Tip:** If you can say *it is*, write *it's*; otherwise write *its*.

cards.title: Choose subject or object pronouns
cards.problem: Correct the sentence: "Between you and I, Abel and me were the only ones who finished."

steps.text: **Step 1: After a preposition use the object form.** "between" is a preposition → between you and **me**.
**Step 2: As the subject of a verb use the subject form.** "Abel and me were" → Abel and **I** were.
**Step 3: Test by removing the other person.** "me were" is wrong; "I was/were" form is right; "between I" is wrong.
**Tip:** cover "you and" or "Abel and" and say the sentence with the pronoun alone.

cards.answer: Between you and me, Abel and I were the only ones who finished.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The scholarship committee awarded the funding to Aster and ________ after reviewing our academic portfolios.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The pronoun follows the preposition 'to' and forms part of a compound prepositional object ('to Aster and [pronoun]'). This slot requires the objective case (Preposition + Object Pronoun).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often write 'Aster and I' because 'Aster and I' is common in the subject position. This is a common pronoun trap in exams. Applying the Cover-Up Test ('awarded the funding to me') makes the correct choice clear.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እቲ ተውላጠ ስም ድሕሪ 'to' ዝብል መስተዋድድ (preposition) ስለ ዝመጸ፡ ኣብቲ ተቐባሊ ሓሳብ (objective case) ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። 'I' (ዋና ባእታ) ኣብዚ ቦታ ክኣቱ ኣይኽእልን እዩ። ነቲ 'Aster and' ዝብል ሓረግ ብምኽዋል 'awarded the funding to me' ኢልና ክነንብቦ ከለና ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'me' (Option B) ምዃኑ ንርዳእ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The old typewriter in the headmaster's office is still functional, but ________ keys are difficult to press.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The blank modifies the noun 'keys' to show ownership. This requires the possessive adjective 'its'.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often confuse 'its' (possessive adjective) with 'it's' (contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'). Option C ('its'') is a non-existent spelling. This spelling distinction is highly tested in national exams.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብዚ ቦታ ናይ ወንነት መግለጺ ቅጽል (possessive adjective) እዩ ዘድልየና። 'Its' (ናቱ/ናታ ንዘይህይወታውያን) ዝብል ቃል ብዘይ ኮማ (apostrophe) ይጸሓፍ። 'It's' ግን ሕጽር ዝበለ ናይ 'it is' ስለ ዝኾነ ኣብዚ ቦታ ኣይሰርሕን እዩ። ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'its' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The teacher asked Ruth and ____ to collect the books.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "Ruth and ___" is the object of "asked".

**Step 2:** Object position needs an object pronoun: me.

**Step 3:** Test: "The teacher asked me".

**Tip:** Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they, who) before a verb and object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them, whom) after verbs and prepositions. Test a compound by removing the other person.

units.title: Verbs
units.intro: Main verbs and helping verbs.

cards.title: Main verbs and helping verbs
rule: A **main verb** tells the action or state: *She **writes**. They **are** happy.* A **helping verb** (*be, have, do*, and modals *can, will, must…*) goes before the main verb: *She **is** writing. They **have** finished. **Do** you know?*

**Regular verbs** add **-ed** for the past and past participle: *work – worked – worked*. **Irregular verbs** change in other ways: *sing – sang – sung, bend – bent – bent, put – put – put*. Learn them from a list.
**be + verb-ing** makes continuous tenses: *She **is working**.* (✗ She working). **be + past participle** makes the passive: *The window **was broken**.*
**have + past participle** makes perfect tenses: *They **have broken** the window.* After a modal use the **base verb**: *She can **swim*** (✗ can swims, can to swim).

examples.text: The children have broken the window.

examples.fix: She is working in a bank.
He can speak French.

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule for this pattern.**
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She go to school every day." breaks this rule.
