cards.title: Notes
body: **In short:** every English sentence needs a verb. Continuous tenses and the passive need a form of **be**.
Three forms to learn for every verb: base – past – past participle (*go – went – gone, write – wrote – written*).
After **do/does/did** and after modals, use the base verb: *Does she **like** it? You must **go**.*

cards.title: Use the correct verb form after modals and auxiliaries
cards.problem: Correct the verbs: "She can sings well, and she has wrote three songs, but she don't like performing."

steps.text: **Step 1: Modal + base form.** can sings → can **sing**.
**Step 2: have/has + past participle.** has wrote → has **written**.
**Step 3: Third-person singular negative uses doesn't + base.** she don't → she **doesn't** like.
**Tip:** after a modal or do/does/did, the main verb never takes -s, -ed or -ing.

cards.answer: She can sing well, and she has written three songs, but she doesn't like performing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular). The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense (has/have + V3).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased' (Option B). However, 'The number of' is singular, requiring the singular auxiliary 'has'. Simple past 'increased' (Option C) is incorrect because the sentence links the past action to the present status.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'the number of' (ቁጽሪ ናይ...) ስለ ዝኾነ ነጸላ (singular) እዩ። ስለዚ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ 'has' (Option A) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'visitors' (ኣጋይሽ) ዝብል ቃል ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ስለ ዝኾነ ተማሃሮ 'have' ብምምራጽ ክጋገዩ ይኽእሉ እዮም።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
This is a direct question in the past simple tense. Questions require subject-auxiliary inversion: Wh-word + auxiliary (didn't) + Subject (you) + base verb (complete).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'. Option B fails to invert the subject and auxiliary. In English, using 'did/didn't' requires the main verb to return to its base form, which is a highly tested rule on exams.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ሕቶ ክንሓትት ከለና እቲ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ ('didn't') ቅድሚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ ('you') ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። ከምኡ ውን 'did' ወይ 'didn't' ምስ ዝህልው፡ እቲ ቀንዲ ግሲ ወትሩ ናብቲ መበቆላዊ ቅጥዑ (base form - 'complete') ክምለስ ኣለዎ። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

units.title: The English Tense System
units.intro: Present simple, present continuous and past.

cards.title: Present simple, present continuous and past
rule: **Present simple** (*I work, she works*) = habits, facts, timetables: *She **walks** to school every day. Water **boils** at 100 °C.*
**Present continuous** (*am/is/are + -ing*) = happening **now** or for a short time: *Look! It**'s raining**. I**'m staying** with my aunt this week.*

**Past simple** (*worked, went*) = finished actions at a past time: *We **visited** Keren last year.* **Past continuous** (*was/were + -ing*) = an action in progress in the past: *I **was reading** when the lights went out.*
**State verbs** (*know, understand, believe, want, like, love, own, seem, belong*) do **not** take -ing: *I **understand** the lesson.* (✗ I am understanding)

cards.title: Notes
body: **Signal words:** present simple – *every day, usually, often, never*; present continuous – *now, at the moment, look!, this week*; past simple – *yesterday, ago, last…*.
Remember the **-s** in the present simple with *he/she/it*: *She work**s***.
State verbs stay simple even "now": *I **know** the answer now.*

cards.title: Present perfect or past simple?
cards.problem: Complete: "I ____ (live) in Keren since 2018. Before that I ____ (live) in Mendefera for six years."

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the time expressions.** "since 2018" links the past to now; "before that … for six years" is a finished period.
**Step 2: Unfinished period up to now → present perfect.** I have lived in Keren since 2018.
**Step 3: Finished period → past simple.** I lived in Mendefera for six years.
**Tip:** since/for + up to now → present perfect; yesterday, ago, in 2015 → past simple.

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The time-marker 'Every morning' indicates a habitual, repeated action in the present. This requires the Present Simple tense (S + V (1/s/es)).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often fail to match the verb to the singular subject 'my father' (3rd person singular), choosing the base form 'drink' (Option C). Option A ('is drinking') is continuous, which is incorrect for habitual actions.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Every morning' (ነፍሲ ወከፍ ንግሆ) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ልሙድ ተግባር (habitual action) ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ Simple Present ክኸውን ኣለዎ። እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'my father' (ነጸላ) ስለ ዝኾነ ድማ እቲ ግሲ 's' ወሲዱ 'drinks' (Option B) ይኸውን።

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The imperative 'Listen!' and 'right now' indicate an action in progress at the exact moment of speaking, requiring the Present Continuous tense (S + am/is/are + V-ing).

Students must identify 'The national choir' as a singular collective noun, which requires the singular auxiliary 'is'. Choosing 'are singing' (Option C) is a common agreement error.

units.title: Perfect tenses and future forms
units.intro: Present perfect, present perfect continuous, past perfect and the future forms (will, going to, present continuous) – explained step by step.

cards.title: Present perfect or past simple?
rule: **Present perfect** = *have/has + past participle*. Use it when the time is **not finished** or **not said**, and the past action matters **now**: *I **have lost** my key* (I still can't find it). *She **has visited** Massawa twice.*
**Past simple** = *verb + -ed / 2nd form*. Use it with a **finished time**: *yesterday, last week, in 2015, two days ago, when I was a child*: *I **lost** my key **yesterday**.*
Time words for the present perfect: *already, yet, just, ever, never, so far, recently, since, for*. ✗ Never use the present perfect with *ago* or *yesterday*.
**since** + the starting point (*since 2019, since Monday, since I came*). **for** + the length of time (*for ten years, for two hours*). ✗ *since ten years*.
**Past perfect** = *had + past participle*: the **earlier** of two past actions: *When we arrived, the film **had started**.*

examples.text: I have finished my homework. Can I go out?
I have finished my project last week.
examples.fix: I finished my project last week.

examples.text: We have lived here for ten years.
She has worked here since five years.
examples.fix: She has worked here for five years.

cards.pattern: have/has + V3 (no finished time)  ·  V2 + finished time  ·  had + V3 (earlier past)

cards.title: Time words: which tense?
head: Time word
Tense
Example
rows: yesterday, last year, ago, in 2015, when…
already, yet, just, ever, never, so far
by the time, before, after (two past actions)
The bus **had left** before we came.
tomorrow, next week + plan with evidence
Look at the clouds! It**'s going to** rain.

cards.title: Present perfect continuous
rule: **Form:** *have/has + been + verb-ing*: *I **have been waiting**. She **has been studying**.* Negative: *haven't/hasn't been + -ing*. Question: *Have you been waiting? How long **has** she **been** studying?*
**Use 1 – an action that started in the past and is still going on**, usually with *for, since, how long, all day*: *Aster **has been working** in this laboratory **since** 2019.*
**Use 2 – an action that has just stopped and we can see the result now**: *I'm tired because I **have been running**. Your eyes are red – **have** you **been crying**?*

**Present perfect vs present perfect continuous:** the continuous shows the **activity / how long**; the simple shows the **result / how many**: *I **have been writing** letters all morning.* (activity) / *I **have written** five letters.* (result, number)
Verbs of state (*know, like, want, believe, understand, own*) do **not** take the continuous: *I **have known** him for years.* ✗ *I have been knowing him.*

examples.text: He has been reading the old manuscript for four hours.

examples.fix: She has been working here since 2019.

examples.text: I have been reading three books this month.
examples.fix: I have read three books this month.

examples.text: I have been knowing her since childhood.
examples.fix: I have known her since childhood.

cards.pattern: have/has + been + V-ing  (+ for / since / how long)

cards.title: Present perfect or present perfect continuous?
head: Present perfect (have + V3)
Present perfect continuous (have been + V-ing)
rows: Result: *I **have painted** the room.* (it is finished)
Activity: *I **have been painting** the room.* (maybe not finished; paint on my hands)
How many / how much: *She **has written** three essays.*
How long: *She **has been writing** for three hours.*
State verbs: *I **have known** him for years.*
✗ not with state verbs (know, like, want, own)
Short or finished actions: *The bus **has arrived**.*
Longer, repeated actions: *It **has been raining** all day.*

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: We ____ for the bus for forty minutes, and it still hasn't come.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *for forty minutes* + *it still hasn't come* → the waiting started in the past and is still going on.

**Step 2:** That is the present perfect continuous: *have been waiting*.

**Step 3:** ✗ *are waiting for forty minutes* – English does not use the present continuous with *for/since* like this.

**Tip:** Action still going on / just stopped + how long (for, since, all day) → have/has been + -ing. Finished result or how many → have/has + past participle.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: I have been drinking four cups of tea today.
options.B: I have drunk four cups of tea today.
options.C: I am drinking four cups of tea today.
options.D: I drank four cups of tea since morning.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *four cups* is a number = a result.

**Step 2:** Results and numbers take the present perfect simple: *have drunk*.

**Step 3:** D: *since* needs a perfect tense, not the past simple.

**Tip:** Action still going on / just stopped + how long (for, since, all day) → have/has been + -ing. Finished result or how many → have/has + past participle.

cards.title: Talk about the future
cards.problem: Choose the best form: (a) "Look at those clouds! It ____ rain." (b) "I ____ meet the doctor at 10 tomorrow – it's booked." (c) "The phone is ringing." – "I ____ answer it."

steps.text: **Step 1: Prediction from present evidence → be going to.** (a) It's going to rain.
**Step 2: Fixed arrangement → present continuous.** (b) I'm meeting the doctor at 10.
**Step 3: Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.** (c) I'll answer it.
**Tip:** ask whether the future is evidence-based, arranged, or decided now.

cards.answer: (a) is going to rain; (b) am meeting; (c) will ('ll) answer.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The time-marker 'since she graduated' indicates an action that started in the past and continues to the present, requiring the Present Perfect Continuous tense (S + has/have been + V-ing).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often see 'is working' (Option A) and choose it because they think of it as an ongoing present action. However, 'since' requires the perfect aspect, making 'has been working' (Option C) correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Since' (ካብቲ...) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ካብ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ጀሚሩ ክሳብ ሕጂ ዝቕጽል ተግባር ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ Present Perfect Continuous ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'Aster' (ነጸላ) ስለ ዝኾነ ድማ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'has been working' (Option C) እዩ።

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The definite past time-marker 'three weeks ago' requires the Simple Past tense (S + V2).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often confuse Present Perfect 'has completed' (Option A) with Simple Past 'completed' (Option B). Present Perfect cannot be used with definite past time-markers like 'three weeks ago'.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Three weeks ago' (ቅድሚ ሰለስተ ሰሙን) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ኣብ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ተፈጺሙ ምውድኡ ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ግሲ ብ Past Simple 'completed' (Option B) ክጸሓፍ ኣለዎ። Present Perfect ምስ 'ago' ክኸይድ ኣይኽእልን እዩ።

units.title: Making questions (direct and indirect)
units.intro: How to make yes/no questions, wh-questions, subject questions and polite indirect questions – four short rules.

cards.title: Four rules for questions
rule: **Yes/no question:** put the helping verb **before** the subject: *She is ready.* → ***Is she** ready?* No helping verb? Use **do / does / did** + base verb: *He plays.* → ***Does he play**?* *They left.* → ***Did they leave**?*
**Wh-question:** wh-word + the yes/no question: *Where **does she live**? Why **did you leave**? What **are** they **doing**?*
**Subject question:** when *who/what* **is** the subject, keep normal order and add no do/does/did: ***Who broke** the window?* (✗ Who did break…?) ***What happened**?*

**Indirect question** (after *Do you know…? Can you tell me…? I wonder… He asked…*): normal order, **no** do/does/did, and **if/whether** for yes/no: *Can you tell me **where the station is**? I asked **if she was** ready.*

cards.title: Form wh-questions about the subject and the object
cards.problem: Ask questions about the underlined words in "Samuel helped Ruth." (a) about Samuel, (b) about Ruth.

steps.text: **Step 1: Subject question – the wh-word replaces the subject, no auxiliary.** (a) Who helped Ruth?
**Step 2: Object question – wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base verb.** (b) Who(m) did Samuel help?
**Step 3: Check the verb form.** In (b) "did" carries the past, so the verb is base "help".
**Tip:** if the answer is the subject, do not add do/does/did.

cards.answer: (a) Who helped Ruth? (b) Who(m) did Samuel help?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Could you please tell me what time ________ from the regional airport tomorrow morning?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
This is an indirect (embedded) question introduced by the polite phrase 'Could you please tell me'. It requires declarative word order: Wh-word (what time) + Subject (the flight) + Verb (departs).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose Option A ('does the flight depart') or Option C ('will the flight depart') because they assume they need direct question inversion. However, indirect questions must not use auxiliary inversion or do/does/did.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እዚ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'Could you please...' ዝጅምር ውሽጣዊ ሕቶ (Indirect/Embedded question) እዩ። ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ውሽጣዊ ሕቶታት ስርዓተ-ሕቶ (inversion) ኣይህልዎምን፤ ልክዕ ከም ስሩዕ ኣዎንታዊ ምሉእ ሓሳብ (Subject + Verb) እዮም ዝጸሓፉ። ስለዚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'the flight' ቅድሚ እቲ ግሲ 'departs' ክስራዕ ኣለዎ (Option B)። 'does the flight depart' ምጥቃም ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why ________ your science project on time last Friday, as the teacher requested?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
This is a direct past Wh-question. It requires the past do/does/did 'didn't' to precede the subject 'you', and the main verb must return to its base form: Why + didn't + Subject + V (base).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'submitted'. Option B fails to invert the subject and auxiliary. Option C correctly uses 'didn't' with the base verb 'submit'.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ቀጥታዊ ሕሉፍ ሕቶ ክንሓትት ከለና እቲ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ ('didn't') ቅድሚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ ('you') ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። ከምኡ ውን 'did' ወይ 'didn't' ምስ ዝህልው፡ እቲ ቀንዲ ግሲ ወትሩ ናብቲ መበቆላዊ ቅጥዑ (base form - 'submit') ክምለስ ኣለዎ። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "Where ____ the keys yesterday?"
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Past simple questions: Wh-word + did + subject + base verb.

**Step 2:** "put" is the base form (and irregular).

**Step 3:** So: Where did you put the keys?

**Tip:** Questions: (Wh-word) + auxiliary + subject + main verb. Subject questions (Who called?) have no auxiliary. Indirect questions use statement word order.

questions.q: Correct the error: "What you are doing?"

why: Direct questions need inversion: auxiliary before subject.

questions.tip: Questions: (Wh-word) + auxiliary + subject + main verb. Subject questions (Who called?) have no auxiliary. Indirect questions use statement word order.

questions.q: ____ book is this? – It's Saba's.
questions.label: 18. ____ book is this? – It's Saba's.

The answer shows possession (Saba's).
"Whose" asks about ownership.

questions.tip: Questions: (Wh-word) + auxiliary + subject + main verb. Subject questions (Who called?) have no auxiliary. Indirect questions use statement word order.

Complete: Nobody knows where he ____ (has gone / has he gone).

why: Answer B: are
After "I wonder whether", use statement order.
So: whether they are ready.

questions.q: True or false: "Which of you knows the answer?" is a correct subject question.

why: True. "Which of you" is the subject of "knows".

questions.tip: Direct question: (wh-word) + auxiliary + subject + verb? Indirect question (after "Do you know…", "He asked…"): wh-word/if + subject + verb, no do/does/did.

questions.q: Could you tell me ____?

similar.q: Make it indirect: "Where is the post office?" (Do you know…)

why: Answer B: how much this costs
After *Could you tell me* the question is indirect.

questions.tip: Direct question: (wh-word) + auxiliary + subject + verb? Indirect question (after "Do you know…", "He asked…"): wh-word/if + subject + verb, no do/does/did.

units.title: Question Tags
units.intro: A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence (…, isn't it?). One table holds all the rules.

cards.title: Question tags: how to make them
rule: A **question tag** is a mini-question at the end of a sentence. We use it to check something or to ask the listener to agree: *It's hot today, **isn't it**?*
**Step 1:** Is the sentence positive or negative? Positive → **negative** tag. Negative → **positive** tag.
**Step 2:** Find the helping verb (*is, are, was, can, will, have, should…*) and repeat it. No helping verb? Use **do / does / did**.
**Step 3:** Use a **pronoun** for the subject: *Aster* → *she*; *the boys* → *they*; *this/that* → *it*.
Learn the special cases in the table: *I am → aren't I*, *Let's → shall we*, orders → *will you*, *never/nobody* → positive tag.

examples.fix: He plays football, doesn't he?

examples.text: I am late, am not I?
examples.fix: I am late, aren't I?

cards.pattern: positive sentence, negative tag?  ·  negative sentence, positive tag?

cards.title: Question tags: key rules
head: Rule
Example
rows: You can swim, **can't you**? He has left, **hasn't he**?
No helping verb → do / does / did
You live here, **don't you**? He played well, **didn't he**?
I'm late, **aren't I**?  (but: I'm not late, **am I**?)
Orders and requests → will you / won't you
never, hardly, seldom, nobody, nothing → positive tag
That was easy, **wasn't it**? Nothing happened, **did it**?

cards.title: Add the correct question tag
cards.problem: Add tags: (a) "You're coming, ___?" (b) "She didn't call, ___?" (c) "Let's go, ___?" (d) "Nobody saw it, ___?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Positive statement → negative tag; negative → positive.**
**Step 2: Repeat the auxiliary and use a pronoun.** (a) aren't you? (b) did she?
**Step 3: Special cases.** "Let's" → shall we? (c). Nobody/no one is negative in meaning and takes "they" → (d) did they?
**Tip:** words like never, nobody and hardly make the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

cards.answer: (a) aren't you? (b) did she? (c) shall we? (d) did they?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Everyone enjoyed the wedding, ____?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Positive sentence → negative tag.

**Step 2:** No helping verb, past → *didn't*.

**Step 3:** *everyone* → *they*.

**Tip:** Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She hardly ever eats meat, ____?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *hardly ever* makes the sentence negative in meaning.

**Step 2:** Negative sentence → positive tag.

**Step 3:** No helping verb, present, *she* → *does she*.

**Tip:** Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Pass me the salt, ____?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** This is an order/request (imperative).

**Step 2:** Orders and requests take *will you?* (or *won't you?* / *could you?*).

**Step 3:** *shall we* is only for *Let's*.

**Tip:** Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular linking verb 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: I am → aren't I?.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose 'am not I' (Option A) because they try to follow the normal positive/negative rule, or 'isn't it' (Option D) due to translation from Tigrinya. Option B 'aren't I' is the correct irregular grammatical exception.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ወግዓዊ ሰዋስው፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'I am' (ኣነ...) ምስ ዝጅምር፡ እቲ ናቱ ፍሉይ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ (question tag) ወትሩ 'aren't I?' (Option B - ኣይኮንኩን?) እዩ ዝኸውን። 'am not I' ምጥቃም ዓቢ ጌጋ እዩ ምኽንያቱ ከምዚ ዝበለ መዋቕር ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ሰዋስው ስለ ዘየለ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple do/does/did (Semi-Negative Statement → Positive Tag).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often see the positive verb spelling 'visits' and automatically select a negative tag like 'doesn't she' (Option A). However, because 'rarely' is negative, the positive tag 'does she' (Option B) is correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Rarely' (ሳሕቲ/ኣዝዩ ውሑድ ግዜ) ዝብል ቃል ኣሉታዊ ቃና (semi-negative) ስለ ዘለዎ፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ከም ኣሉታዊ ይውሰድ። ስለዚ እቲ ዝስዕብ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ ብኣዎንታዊ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ 'does she' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'doesn't she' ምምራጽ ናይዚ ሕጊ መጻወድያ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely ever goes to cinema_______?
cards.why: The word 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the whole sentence negative. Negative sentences require positive question tags. Since the verb is 'goes' (Present Simple), the tag is 'does she'.

questions.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
questions.label: 1. I am late for the registration of the national matriculation
why: Answer B: aren't I
The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular linking verb 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: I am → aren't I?.

questions.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
questions.label: 2. She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long ac
why: Answer B: does she

The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple do/does/did (Semi-Negative Statement → Positive Tag).

questions.q: Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholarship announcement, ________?
questions.label: 3. Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholars
why: Answer B: weren't they

Indefinite pronouns referring to people ('everyone') require the plural pronoun 'they' in the tag. Because the pronoun is plural, the past linking verb 'was' must shift to plural 'weren't' to maintain agreement.

questions.q: Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the final lecture begins, ________?
questions.label: 4. Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the fina
why: Answer B: shall we
Suggestions starting with 'Let's' (contraction of 'Let us') require the irregular question tag 'shall we?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: She doesn't speak French fluently, ________?
questions.label: 5. She doesn't speak French fluently, ________?
why: Answer B: does she
The main clause is negative ('doesn't speak'). This requires a positive question tag using the matching auxiliary 'does': Negative Statement → Positive Tag.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label:
6. Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Spe
why: Answer A: So do I.

Speaker A's statement is positive and in the Simple Present tense (no auxiliary present). Speaker B wants to show agreement, requiring the inverted positive agreement structure: So + do/does + Subject.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label: 7. Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.'
why: Answer B: Neither do I.
Speaker A's statement is negative ('don't like'). To show agreement with a negative statement, Speaker B must use the inverted negative agreement structure: Neither/Nor + Auxiliary + Subject.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment, ________?
questions.label: 8. Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment,
why: Answer A: did it
The subject 'Nothing' is negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with past simple do/does/did and the singular pronoun 'it'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress, ________?
questions.label: 9. Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress,
why: Answer B: will you
Negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't') strictly require the positive tag 'will you?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The university dean has already signed the official graduation list, ________?
questions.label: 10. The university dean has already signed the official graduati
why: Answer B: hasn't he

The main clause contains the positive perfect auxiliary 'has' ('has already signed'). This requires a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary 'hasn't' and pronoun 'he': Positive Statement → Negative Tag.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Punctuation marks are very important in writing, _______?
why: Answer E: aren't they

To form a question tag:
1. Use the auxiliary verb from the statement ('are').
2. If the statement is positive, the tag must be negative ('aren't').
3. Use the pronoun that corresponds to the subject ('Punctuation marks' = 'they').
Result: **'aren't they'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: None of the students is trying, ___________?
why: Answer C: Are they
The word 'None' makes the sentence negative, so the question tag must be positive. Since 'students' is plural, the pronoun 'they' is used. Therefore, 'Are they' is the correct tag.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Selam: I hope it is going to be a minor surgery, **61**?
why: Answer B: isn't it
**Rule:** A question tag uses the auxiliary verb from the main sentence. Since the main sentence is positive ('it **is** going to be'), the tag must be negative: **'isn't it?'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Only two students understood the instruction, ___?
why: Answer A: didn't they
The main sentence is positive and in the Simple Past ('understood'). Therefore, the question tag must be negative and use the auxiliary 'did' ('didn't they').
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Suleman: This coat looks nice for such a chilly weather, __________?
why: Answer D: doesn't it
**Rule:** For a positive statement in Present Simple ("This coat looks"), the tag must be negative using the auxiliary 'do/does'. Since "coat" is singular, we use "doesn't it".
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Open the door_______?
why: Answer D: will you
For imperative sentences (commands or requests), 'will you' is the most common and standard question tag used to invite cooperation.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Don't open the question paper until you are told to do so, _____________?
why: Answer D: Will you
For negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't'), the standard question tag is 'will you'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All the teachers are working hard this semester, (38) ______.
why: Answer B: so are the students
To add a positive statement that agree with a previous positive statement, we use 'so + auxiliary verb + subject'. Since the first clause uses 'are', the addition is 'so are the students'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Nobody phoned while I was out, ____?
questions.label: 19. Nobody phoned while I was out, ____?
why: Answer D: did they
"Nobody" makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.
Indefinite pronouns like nobody/everyone take "they" in the tag.
Past simple → did: did they?
questions.tip: Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. Use the same auxiliary (or do/does/did). Special: I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we.

questions.q: You'd better leave now, ____?
questions.label: 20. You'd better leave now, ____?
why: Answer D: hadn't you
"You'd better" = "You had better".
The auxiliary is "had", so the tag uses "hadn't".
So: You'd better leave now, hadn't you?
questions.tip: Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. Use the same auxiliary (or do/does/did). Special: I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we.

questions.q: There isn't any water left, ____?
why: Answer B: is there
Negative sentence → positive tag.
*There is* → tag with *there*: *is there?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

questions.q: Your brother works in Massawa, ____?
why: Answer B: doesn't he
Positive, no helping verb, present, *he* → *doesn't he?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

questions.q: Nothing can stop us now, ____?
why: Answer B: can it
*Nothing* is negative → positive tag.
*Nothing* → *it*; repeat *can*: *can it?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

questions.q: You won't forget to call me, ____?
why: Negative sentence (*won't*) → positive tag *will you?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

questions.q: I'm in the right room, ____?
why: Special case: *I am* → *aren't I?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

questions.q: Correct the tag: "They had a good time, hadn't they?"
accept: didn't they?
They had a good time, didn't they
questions.answer: They had a good time, didn't they?
why: Here *had* is the main verb (= enjoyed), not a helping verb.
Main verb in the past → *didn't they?*
questions.tip: Positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. Repeat the helping verb (no helping verb → do/does/did) and use a pronoun.

units.title: Word formation: prefixes, suffixes, compounds
units.intro: We make new words in four simple ways: add a prefix, add a suffix, join two words (compound), or use the same word as a new word class (conversion).

cards.title: Four ways to make new words
rule: **1. Prefix** = letters added at the **start** of a word. It changes the **meaning**: *happy → **un**happy, write → **re**write, agree → **dis**agree*.

**2. Suffix** = letters added at the **end** of a word. It usually changes the **word class**: *depart (verb) → depart**ure** (noun), care (noun) → care**ful** (adjective), quick → quick**ly** (adverb)*.
**3. Compound** = two words joined to make one: *class + room → **classroom**, black + board → **blackboard**, mother-in-law, bus stop*.
**4. Conversion** = the **same word** used as a different word class, with no change: *a **text** (noun) → to **text** someone (verb); a **book** → to **book** a room*.

**How to answer word-formation questions:** look at the gap. After *a/an/the* or an adjective → **noun**. Before a noun or after *be/seem* → **adjective**. Telling *how* → **adverb**. Then choose the right ending.

examples.text: The sudden departure of the principal surprised everyone.

examples.fix: The instructions were unclear.
She sings beautifully.

cards.pattern: prefix + word  ·  word + suffix  ·  word + word  ·  same word, new class

cards.title: Step by step: choose the right form
cards.problem: Complete: "The ____ (develop) of the town was ____ (success) because the people worked ____ (careful)."

steps.text: **Step 1: What does each gap need?** After *The* → noun. After *was* → adjective. After the verb *worked*, telling how → adverb.
**Step 2: Add the ending.** develop + -ment → **development**; success + -ful → **successful**; careful + -ly → **carefully**.
**Step 3: Read the sentence again** to check the meaning and spelling.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The opposite of "legal" is ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** All four prefixes can mean *not*.

**Step 2:** Before a word starting with **l** we use **il-**: *illegal, illogical*.

**Step 3:** Before **r** → *ir-* (irregular); before **m/p** → *im-* (impossible).

**Tip:** First decide which word class the gap needs (noun after a/the, adjective before a noun or after be, adverb for how). Then add the suffix. Prefixes change the meaning, not the word class.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which word is a compound?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** A compound joins two complete words.

**Step 2:** *class + room = classroom*.

**Step 3:** A has a suffix, B a prefix, D a suffix.

**Tip:** First decide which word class the gap needs (noun after a/the, adjective before a noun or after be, adverb for how). Then add the suffix. Prefixes change the meaning, not the word class.

cards.title: Build words with affixes
cards.problem: Complete with a form of the word in brackets: "The plan was ____ (success) because the team was ____ (organise) and ____ (honest) was rewarded."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the needed word class.** After "was" and before "because" → adjective; after "was" describing the team → adjective (participle); subject of a verb → noun.
**Step 2: Add the suffix.** success + -ful → successful; organise + -ed → organised; honest + -y → honesty.
**Step 3: Check the meaning and spelling.**
**Tip:** -ful/-ous/-ive make adjectives; -ness/-ity/-ment/-y make nouns; un-/dis-/in- change the meaning, not the class.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The sudden ________ of the school principal surprised both the teachers and the students.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The blank follows the article 'The' and the adjective 'sudden', requiring a noun (Article + Adjective + Noun).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose the verb 'depart' (Option A) due to direct translation. Only the noun form 'departure' (Option B), formed by adding the suffix '-ure' to the verb 'depart', is grammatically correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**

units.title: Phrasal Verbs
units.intro: Phrasal verbs.

cards.title: Phrasal verbs
rule: A **phrasal verb** = verb + a small word (*up, off, out, down, on, after*). The meaning is often new: *give up* = stop trying, *call off* = cancel, *look after* = take care of, *run into* = meet by chance.
**Separable** phrasal verbs: a noun object can go after or in the middle: *turn off the light* / *turn the light off*.
With a **pronoun** (*it, them, him*), the pronoun **must** go in the middle: *turn **it** off* (✗ turn off it), *write **them** down*.
**Inseparable** ones never split: *look after the children / look after **them*** (✗ look them after); also *rely on, cope with, run into, get over*.

examples.fix: Please turn it off.

examples.text: She looks after her little brother.
The match was called off because of the rain.

cards.pattern: verb + particle + noun  ·  verb + pronoun + particle

cards.title: Notes
body: **In short:** learn each phrasal verb with its meaning, like a new word.
Pronoun object → put it in the middle of a separable phrasal verb: *pick **it** up, put **them** away*.
Common ones in exams: give up, call off, put off (postpone), look forward to + -ing, run out of, get on with, take after (look like a parent).

cards.problem: Because of the heavy rainfall and flooding, the school principal had to ________ the sports competition.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The context 'heavy rainfall and flooding' indicates that the sports competition had to be canceled.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because of the heavy rainfall and flooding, the school principal had to ________ the sports competition.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The context 'heavy rainfall and flooding' indicates that the sports competition had to be canceled. We need a phrasal verb meaning to cancel.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often confuse 'put off' (to postpone) with 'call off' (to cancel). While both are common, 'call off' (Option B) is the correct phrasal verb meaning to cancel an event.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Call off' (ምስራዝ) ዝብል ቅጽል ግሲ ንሓደ መደብ ወይ ውድድር ምሉእ ብምሉእ ንምስራዝ የገልግል። 'Put off' (ምስጋጋር) ግን ሓደ መደብ ንኻልእ ግዜ ምስጋጋር ንምግላጽ እዩ። ኣብዚ ብሰንኪ ውሕጅን ከቢድ ዝናብን እቲ ውድድር ስለ ዝተሰረዘ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'call off' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option B 'hand in it' places the pronoun at the end, which violates the pronoun separation rule. Option D 'hand it down' has an incorrect meaning (to pass to next generation). Option C is correct.

units.title: Prepositions
units.intro: Prepositions of place, time and movement in simple tables, the most common mistakes, then the word + preposition pairs you must learn by heart.

lessons.title: Prepositions of place, time and movement

cards.title: What is a preposition?
rule: A **preposition** is a small word before a noun or pronoun. It shows **where** (*in the box*), **when** (*on Monday*) or **how something moves** (*into the room*).
**at, on, in** are the most common. Think of size: **at** = a point, **on** = a surface or a day, **in** = inside or a longer time.
After a preposition use a **noun**, an **object pronoun** (*me, him, them*) or a verb + **-ing**: *with **him**, before **leaving*** (✗ before leave).
Many words have a fixed partner: *good **at**, interested **in**, depend **on***. Learn them as pairs (see 18.2).

examples.text: The meeting is at 3 o'clock on Friday.

examples.fix: I was born in 2008.
He entered the room. / He went into the room.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The school year in Eritrea usually starts ____ September.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *September* is a month.

**Step 2:** Months, years and seasons take **in**.

**Step 3:** For a date we would say *on 1 September*.

**Tip:** at = a point (at 6, at the door); on = a surface / a day (on the table, on Monday); in = inside / a longer period (in the box, in May, in 2026).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The children ran ____ the classroom when the bell rang.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *ran* shows movement.

**Step 2:** Leaving an inside place → **out of**.

**Step 3:** *at* and *on* show position, not movement.

**Tip:** at = a point (at 6, at the door); on = a surface / a day (on the table, on Monday); in = inside / a longer period (in the box, in May, in 2026).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I'll meet you ____ the bus stop ____ 4 o'clock.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *the bus stop* is a point → **at**.

**Step 2:** Clock times → **at**.

**Step 3:** So: *at the bus stop at 4 o'clock*.

**Tip:** at = a point (at 6, at the door); on = a surface / a day (on the table, on Monday); in = inside / a longer period (in the box, in May, in 2026).

cards.title: Word + preposition: learn them as pairs
body: Some verbs, adjectives and nouns always go with the **same** preposition. We cannot guess it from Tigrinya, so learn each word **with** its partner.
**Adjective + preposition:** good/bad **at**, interested **in**, afraid/proud/tired **of**, famous **for**, angry **with** (a person), married **to**, different **from**.
**Verb + preposition:** depend/rely **on**, congratulate someone **on**, accuse someone **of**, suffer **from**, listen **to**, belong **to**, wait **for**, apologise **for**.
**Noun + preposition:** the reason **for**, the key/answer/solution **to**, an increase **in**, a cause **of**.
After these prepositions a verb takes **-ing**: *interested in **learning**, congratulated on **passing**.*

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The school principal warmly congratulated the top-performing students ________ achieving straight A's in the national exam.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The verb 'congratulate' requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: congratulate + someone + on + something.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often choose 'for' because they translate 'ብምሓለፍካ' (for your passing) directly into English.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The school principal warmly congratulated the top-performing students ________ achieving straight A's in the national exam.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The verb 'congratulate' requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: congratulate + someone + on + something.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose 'for' (Option A) because they translate 'ብምሓለፍካ' (for your passing) directly into English. This is a classic direct translation from Tigrinya trap on national examinations. Option B is correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Congratulate' (እንኳዕ ሓጎሰካ ምባል) ዝብል ግሲ ወግዒ ወትሩ ምስ 'on' ዝብል መስተዋድድ ጥራይ እዩ ዝስዕብ (congratulate on - Option B)። ተማሃሮ 'ብምሓለፍካ' ንምባል 'for' (Option A) ብምጥቃም ክጋገዩ ይረኣዩ እዮም፤ እዚ ግን ዓቢ ናይ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.problem: Aster has always been exceptionally clever ________ mathematics and chemistry, which is why she wants to study engineering.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Adjectives describing skill or proficiency (like *good, bad, clever, expert*) must strictly be paired with the preposition 'at' (clever + at + subject).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often choose 'in' because they translate the Tigrinya locative prefix 'ኣብ' (in math) directly into English.

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The regional government is trying to find a viable solution ________ the severe water shortage in our town.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Nouns representing entries, answers, or solutions (like *solution, key, answer, response*) strictly require the preposition 'to' (solution + to + noun).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often choose 'of' because they translate possessive phrases like 'ናይዚ ጸገም መፍትሕ' (the key of this problem) directly, resulting in the incorrect use of 'of'.

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
Nouns representing entries, answers, or solutions (like *solution, key, answer, response*) strictly require the preposition 'to' (solution + to + noun).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose 'of' (Option A) because they translate possessive phrases like 'ናይዚ ጸገም መፍትሕ' (the key of this problem) directly, resulting in the incorrect use of 'of'. Option B is correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Solution' (መፍትሒ) ዝብል ስም ወትሩ ድሕሪኡ 'to' ዝብል መስተዋድድ እዩ ዝወስድ (solution to the problem - Option B)። 'of' ምጥቃም ናይ ትግርኛ 'ናይ...' ዝብል መዋቕር ቀጥታዊ ትርጉም ስለ ዝኾነ ሰዋስዋዊ ጌጋ ይፈጥር።

why: Days → **on** (*on Monday*).

units.title: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions
units.intro: Collocations, idioms and similes.

cards.title: Collocations, idioms and similes
rule: A **collocation** is a pair of words that naturally go together: *make a decision, do homework, commit a crime, pay attention, take an exam, keep a promise, heavy rain, strong tea*.
You cannot translate them word for word. ✗ *do a decision, give attention, strong rain*.
An **idiom** has a meaning different from its words: *break the ice* = start a friendly conversation; *once in a blue moon* = very rarely; *a piece of cake* = very easy.
A **simile** compares with **as … as** or **like**: *as busy as a bee, as brave as a lion, sleep like a log*.

body: **make** = create (a decision, a mistake, a plan, progress, noise); **do** = activity/work (homework, the dishes, an exercise, your best).

Idioms are used in speaking and stories; in formal essays use plain words.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The noun 'progress' requires the verb 'make' to form the standard English collocation: make + progress.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because of the ________ rain, the regional football championship was postponed until next week.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The noun 'rain' is modified by the adjective 'heavy' to describe high volume, forming the fixed collocation: heavy + rain.

units.title: Synonyms, Antonyms, Analogies
units.intro: Synonyms, antonyms and analogies.

cards.title: Synonyms, antonyms and analogies
rule: A **synonym** has the same or nearly the same meaning: *big – large, begin – start, brave – courageous*. Choose the one that fits the **sentence**.
An **antonym** has the opposite meaning: *hot – cold, ancient – modern*. Many are made with a prefix: *possible – **im**possible, honest – **dis**honest, compatible – **in**compatible*.
Use **context clues**: words like *however, but, although, whereas* often show an opposite meaning; *and, also, in other words* show a similar meaning.
An **analogy** compares two pairs that have the same relationship: *hand : glove :: foot : sock* (what you wear on it). Find the link in the first pair, then apply it to the second.
Word parts help: *bene-* = good, *mal-* = bad, *chron-* = time, *auto-* = self: *benefit, malnutrition, chronological, autobiography*.

examples.fix: "Ancient" is the antonym of "modern".

cards.pattern: synonym = same · antonym = opposite · A : B :: C : D (same link)

cards.title: Notes
body: **Exam method:** read the whole sentence, cover the options, think of your own word, then choose the option closest to it.
Check the word class: a noun must be replaced by a noun, an adjective by an adjective.
For analogies, say the link as a sentence: "A glove is worn on a hand" → "A sock is worn on a foot".

cards.problem: The effects of the traditional medicine were ________, lasting only a few minutes before the pain returned.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The context 'lasting only a few minutes' indicates that the effects were short-lived, requiring an adjective meaning temporary.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often confuse 'potent' (powerful) or 'inevitable' (unavoidable) with the correct option.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The effects of the traditional medicine were ________, lasting only a few minutes before the pain returned.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The context 'lasting only a few minutes' indicates that the effects were short-lived, requiring an adjective meaning temporary.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often confuse 'potent' (powerful) or 'inevitable' (unavoidable) with the correct option. 'Ephemeral' (Option B) is the precise academic synonym for short-lived.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Ephemeral' (ሳሕቲ/ኣዝዩ ሕጽር ዝበለ ግዜ ዝጸንሕ) ዝብል ቃል፡ ንሓጺር እዋን ጥራይ ዝጸንሕ ኩነታት ንምግላጽ የገልግል። እቲ ሓረግ 'lasting only a few minutes' (ንሒደት ደቓይቕ ጥራይ ዝጸንሐ) ስለ ዝበለ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The contrastive conjunction 'Unlike' indicates that the blank must contain the antonym of 'malevolent' (evil-wishing/cruel).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

units.title: Conversational English, Dialogue Completion
units.intro: Everyday conversation: useful expressions.

cards.title: Everyday conversation: useful expressions
rule: In dialogue questions, first decide the **function**: agreeing, disagreeing, inviting, refusing, apologising, thanking, advising, complaining.
**Strong agreement:** *I couldn't agree more! / You can say that again!* (both mean "I agree completely", even though one has *not*).
**Polite refusal:** *I'd love to, but… / I'm afraid I can't.* **Thanks:** *Thank you – You're welcome / Not at all / Don't mention it.*
**Apology:** *I'm sorry I'm late. – That's all right / Never mind.* **Advice:** *You'd better… / Why don't you…? / If I were you, I would…*

examples.text: A: Thank you for your help. B: You're welcome.
A: I'm sorry I'm late. B: Yes, I'm sorry too.
examples.fix: B: That's all right.

examples.text: A: This exam was very hard. B: You can say that again!

cards.pattern: function → formula: agree · refuse · thank · apologise · advise

cards.title: Notes
body: **Exam method:** read the line **after** the gap too – it often shows if the answer was yes or no.
Polite English uses *Could you…? Would you mind + -ing? I'm afraid…*.
Some answers look negative but are positive: *I couldn't agree more. Not at all* (= you're welcome / no problem).

cards.problem:
Speaker A: 'The new school principal is exceptionally supportive and fair.'
Speaker B: '________ He has already resolved several student complaints.'

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Speaker A makes a positive statement.
Speaker B's following sentence ('He has already resolved...') confirms strong agreement.
We need a standard expression of strong agreement.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Speaker A: 'The new school principal is exceptionally supportive and fair.'
Speaker B: '________ He has already resolved several student complaints.'
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
Speaker A makes a positive statement. Speaker B's following sentence ('He has already resolved...') confirms strong agreement. We need a standard expression of strong agreement.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often avoid 'I couldn't agree more!' (Option A) because they see the negative modal 'couldn't' and assume it means disagreement. This is a classic pragmatic trap. In English, 'I couldn't agree more!' means complete agreement.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
Speaker A 'እቲ ርእሰ-መምህር ንፉዕ እዩ' ኢሉ ሓሳቡ ክገልጽ ከሎ፡ Speaker B ድማ 'ብምሉእ ሓሳብካ እሰማማዕ እየ' ክብል ይደሊ ኣሎ (እቲ ዝሰዓበ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ነዚ የረጋግጽ)። ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ፍጹም ስምምዕ ንምግላጽ 'I couldn't agree more!' (Option A - ካብዚ ንላዕሊ ክሰማማዕ ኣይክእልን/ምሉእ ብምሉእ እሰማማዕ) ንጥቀም።

Speaker B: '________ I have to complete my biology assignment before tomorrow.'

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Speaker A extends an invitation.

cards.q:
Speaker A: 'Would you like to attend the graduation party at our house tonight?'
Speaker B: '________ I have to complete my biology assignment before tomorrow.'

options.D: I am sorry to hear that,

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
Speaker A extends an invitation. Speaker B provides a reason for declining ('I have to complete my assignment...'). This requires a polite refusal formula: Appreciation + but + Reason.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Option A is too direct and impolite. Option C accepts but contradicts the following clause. Option B 'I'd love to, but' is the correct polite refusal formula.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ዕድመ ብትሕትና ንምእባይ (polite refusal) እንጥቀመሉ ናይ ዝርርብ ቀመር 'I'd love to, but...' (Option B - ደስ ምበለኒ ነይሩ ግን...) እዩ። 'No, I don't want to' (Option A) ምጥቃም ግን ብባህሊ እንግሊዘኛ ዘይልሙድን ብዕሉግን ተገይሩ እዩ ዝውሰድ።

Speaker B: '________ consult the academic counselor before making a final decision?'

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The blank is followed by a base verb 'consult' and ends with a question mark. This requires the suggestion formula: Why don't you + V (base) … ?

Option B lacks the question format. Option C 'You'd better to' incorrectly inserts 'to' after 'better'. Option A 'Why don't you' is correct and natural.

cards.title: Pronunciation: vowel sounds and silent letters
rule: English spelling and sound do not always match: *ough* sounds different in *cough, through, though, enough*.

**Silent letters:** *b* after *m* (*climb, thumb, comb*) and in *debt, doubt*; *k* before *n* (*know, knife*); *w* before *r* (*write, wrong*); *h* in *hour, honest*; *t* in *listen, castle*; *g* before *n* (*sign, foreign*).
**Short and long vowels:** *ship /ɪ/ – sheep /iː/, full /ʊ/ – fool /uː/, cat /æ/ – cart /ɑː/*. Changing the vowel can change the word.
The **-ed** ending has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless sounds (*walked, watched*), /d/ after voiced sounds (*played, lived*), /ɪd/ after t or d (*wanted, needed*).

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
Silent 'h' occurs in words of French origin such as 'honest', 'hour', and 'honor'. In 'house', 'h' is a fully voiced glottal fricative (/haʊs/).

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
In 'chef', 'machine', and 'brochure', the 'ch' is pronounced as `/ʃ/` (French origin). In 'choir', it is pronounced as `/k/` followed by a glide (/kwaɪər/).

'Chef', 'machine',ን 'brochure'ን ናይ ፈረንሳይ መበቆል ስለ ዘለዎም እቲ 'ch' ከም 'ሾ' (/ʃ/) ይድመጽ። 'Choir' (መዘምራን) ግን ክንብብ ከለና 'ኳየር' (/kwaɪər/) ስለ ዝበሃል ፍሉይ ኣደማምጻ ኣለዎ (Option D)።

units.title: Reading Comprehension, Context Clues
units.intro: Reading: main idea, details and reference words.

cards.title: Reading: main idea, details and reference words
rule: **Skimming** = read quickly (title, first and last sentence of each paragraph) to find the **main idea**.
**Scanning** = look quickly for one fact: a name, a number, a date.
**Context clues** for new words: a definition (*…, which means…*), an example (*such as…*), a synonym (*or…*), or an opposite (*but, however*).
**Reference words** (*it, they, this, that, these, which, the former, the latter*) point back to a noun before them. Replace the word with your answer and read the sentence again to check.

examples.text: Skimming means reading for the main idea.
Scanning means reading every word slowly.
examples.fix: Scanning means looking quickly for a particular fact.

cards.pattern: skim → main idea · scan → detail · reference word → the noun before it

cards.title: Notes
body: **Exam method:** read the questions first, then read the passage.
For a "meaning of the word" question, read the sentence before and after the word.
For a "what does it refer to" question, look back at the nouns just before the word.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** 'It' is a singular neuter subject pronoun.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Read the context and answer the question:
'The ministry launched a new educational portal last week. **It** was designed to provide free learning modules for high school students.'
The pronoun 'It' refers to:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'It' is a singular neuter subject pronoun. Its antecedent must be a singular inanimate noun phrase mentioned in the preceding sentence.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students might choose 'the ministry' (singular) or 'free learning modules' (plural). By applying the Pronoun Substitution Test ('The new educational portal was designed to...'), Option B is clearly correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'It' (ንሱ - ዘይህይወታዊ ነጸላ) ዝብል ተውላጠ ስም ንሓደ ቅድሚኡ ዝተገልጸ ነጸላ ስም እዩ ዝውክል። ነቲ ሓረግ 'The new educational portal was designed...' (እቲ ሓድሽ መርበብ ሓበሬታ...) ኢልና ክንተክኦ ከለና ግቡእ ትርጉም ስለ ዝህብ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Choose the closest contextual meaning of the underlined word:
'The professor's lecture was exceptionally **succinct**; he covered the entire complex topic in only five minutes.'
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The context clue 'in only five minutes' indicates that the lecture was very short and concise. We need a synonym for 'succinct'.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often guess 'detailed' (Option A) because of 'complex topic'. However, the time clue ('five minutes') confirms that 'brief' (Option B) is the correct meaning.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Succinct' (ሓጺርን ንጹርን) ዝብል ቃል፡ ንሓደ ተግባር ብሓጺርን ብቑርጥን መገዲ ክግለጽ ከሎ የውክል ኩነታዊ መርትዖና ድማ 'in only five minutes' (ንሓሙሽተ ደቓይቕ ጥራይ) ዝብል ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ቅኑዕ ትርጉሙ 'brief' (Option B - ሓጺር) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Read the context and answer the question:
'The candidates completed their laboratory tests. The program coordinator congratulated them on **their** outstanding results.'
The possessive pronoun 'their' refers to:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Their' is a plural possessive pronoun. It must refer back to a plural noun denoting owners, which is 'candidates' (the people who achieved the results).

The speech "lasted two hours" but "said very little that was new".

questions.label: 16. Read: "Hagos was usually gregarious, chatting with everyone at parties, but after his father's…

units.title: Common Grammatical Mistakes
units.intro: Common mistakes (and how to fix them).

cards.title: Common mistakes (and how to fix them)
rule: **Double subject:** ✗ *My father he is a teacher.* → *My father is a teacher.*
**Two linking words for one idea:** ✗ *Although it rained, but we went out.* → use only one: *Although it rained, we went out.* / *It rained, but we went out.*
**Missing *is/are*:** ✗ *She very clever.* → *She **is** very clever.*
**Comparatives and superlatives:** ✗ *more better, most cleverest* → *better, cleverest*; ✗ *She is the most intelligent than…* → *more intelligent than* / *the most intelligent in…*.
**Word order:** subject + verb + object: ✗ *Our team the final won.* → *Our team won the final.*

examples.text: My father he is a teacher.
examples.fix: My father is a teacher.

examples.text: Although it was raining, but we went out.
examples.fix: Although it was raining, we went out.

examples.text: This book is better than that one.

cards.pattern: S + V + O · one linking word · better / the best

cards.title: Notes
body: **Checklist before you hand in:** Is there a verb? Only one subject? One linking word per idea? -s with he/she/it?
Many mistakes come from translating Tigrinya word by word. Read your sentence aloud in English.
Compare with *-er / more … than*; use *the -est / the most* with *in / of*.

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct and free from double-subject mistakes?

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** In English, a clause must contain only a single subject referent per verb.
The noun phrase 'My elder brother' is the subject of 'is studying'.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

cards.answer: My elder brother is studying civil engineering at university.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct and free from double-subject mistakes?

options.A: My elder brother he is studying civil engineering at university.
options.B: My elder brother is studying civil engineering at university.
options.C: My elder brother, he is studying civil engineering at university.
options.D: My elder brother him is studying civil engineering at university.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
In English, a clause must contain only a single subject referent per verb. The noun phrase 'My elder brother' is the subject of 'is studying'.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Options A and C contain a redundant pronoun 'he' immediately following the noun subject. This is a classic double-subject error caused by Tigrinya verb conjugation habits. Option B correctly eliminates the redundant pronoun.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ወግዒ ሓደ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ሓደ ዋና ባእታ (Subject) ጥራይ እዩ ዝወስድ። 'My elder brother' (ሓወይ) ባዕሉ እኹል ዋና ባእታ ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ድሕሪኡ 'he' (ንሱ) ምጥቃም ድርብ ዋና ባእታ (Double Subject) ዝበሃል ዓቢ ጌጋ ይፈጥር። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoon, ________ we were unable to perform the experiment.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses.
In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoon, ________ we were unable to perform the experiment.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Because' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses. In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often choose 'so' (Option A) because in Tigrinya, it is natural to pair cause with result (e.g., 'ስለ ዝሓመመ፡ ስለዚ...'). Option D is correct because no extra connector is allowed.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብ መጀመርታ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ 'Because' (ምኽንያቱ/ስለ ዝ-) ዝብል መተሓሓዚ ስለ ዘሎ፡ ኣብቲ ካልኣይ ሓረግ 'so' (ስለዚ) ምጥቃም ዓቢ ናይ ድርብ መስተጻምር ጌጋ (double-conjunction error) ይፈጥር። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option D ([No connector] - ዋላ ሓደ ቃል ኣየድልይን) እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Which sentence is missing a linking verb (is/am/are/was/were)?

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires a linking verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** In Option C, the linking verb 'is' is completely missing.

cards.answer: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence is missing a linking verb (is/am/are/was/were)?

options.A: She is an exceptionally clever student in our class.
options.B: They are from the southern region of Eritrea.
options.C: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.
options.D: We were delighted to receive your invitation.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires a linking verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
In Option C, the linking verb 'is' is completely missing. In Tigrinya, the linking verb can sometimes be omitted in speech, leading students to translate directly as 'My brother very hardworking...', which is incorrect. Option C is the target error.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ 'ምዃን' ዘመልክቱ ሓገዝቲ ግሶች (linking verbs - is, are) ወግዒ ክጸሓፉ ኣለዎም። ኣብ Option C 'My brother [is] very hardworking' ክኸውን ስለ ዝነበሮ፡ እቲ ግሲ ብምጥፋኡ ጌጋ ኣለዎ። ተማሃሮ ብስሕተት 'My brother very...' ኢሎም ክጽሕፉ ይረኣዩ እዮም።

Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires a linking verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.

questions.q: The program coordinator congratulated the candidates ________ achieving top scores in the national exam.
questions.label: 4. The program coordinator congratulated the candidates _______
why: Answer B: on
The verb 'congratulate' strictly requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: congratulate + someone + on + something.

questions.q: The administrative assistant provided us with many useful ________ regarding the registration process.
questions.label: 5. The administrative assistant provided us with many useful __
why: Answer B: pieces of advice
'Advice' is strictly uncountable and cannot be pluralized with an '-s' suffix. To express plurality, we must use partitive phrases like 'pieces of advice'.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

similar.q: Correct: He gave me an advice.
similar.a: He gave me some advice / a piece of advice.

questions.q: Identify the sentence that displays correct pronoun placement for a separable phrasal verb:
questions.label: 6. Identify the sentence that displays correct pronoun placemen

options.A: Please turn off the light before you leave.
options.B: Please turn the light off before you leave.
options.C: Please turn it off before you leave.
options.D: Please turn off it before you leave.

why: Answer D: Please turn off it before you leave.
'Turn off' is a transitive separable phrasal verb. Noun objects can go in the middle or at the end. Pronoun objects ('it') **must** go in the middle: Verb + Pronoun + Particle.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

similar.q: Correct: Please suggest me a book.
similar.a: Please suggest a book to me.

questions.q: The chemistry instructor told the students ________ any of the chemical solutions.
questions.label: 7. The chemistry instructor told the students ________ any of t
why: Answer B: not to touch
This is a reported negative command. Negative commands are reported using the structure: reporting verb + object + not to + V (base).
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: Choose the sentence that displays correct English word order (S-V-O):
questions.label: 8. Choose the sentence that displays correct English word order

options.A: The doctor the patient examined yesterday afternoon.
options.B: The doctor examined the patient yesterday afternoon.
options.C: Yesterday afternoon the doctor the patient examined.
options.D: Examined the doctor the patient yesterday afternoon.

why: Answer B: The doctor examined the patient yesterday afternoon.
English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object (S-V-O) pattern. The subject is 'The doctor', the verb is 'examined', and the direct object is 'the patient'.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: When I was a young boy living in the village, I was extremely afraid ________ wild dogs.
questions.label: 9. When I was a young boy living in the village, I was extremel
why: Answer C: of
The adjective 'afraid' must strictly be paired with the preposition 'of' (afraid + of + noun).
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: Identify the option that displays correct spelling for the modified word class:
questions.label: 10. Identify the option that displays correct spelling for the m

options.A: We had a delicious lunch in the school dinning room.
options.B: We had a delicious lunch in the school dining room.
options.C: We had a delicious lunch in the school daining room.
options.D: We had a delicious lunch in the school dineing room.

why: Answer B: We had a delicious lunch in the school dining room.
The verb 'dine' ends in a single silent 'e'. When adding the suffix '-ing', the 'e' is dropped to form 'dining' (/ˈdaɪnɪŋ/).
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.label: 11. Which sentence is correct?

options.B: I don't knows anything about it.
options.C: I don't know nothing about it.
options.D: I don't know anything about it.

why: Answer D: I don't know anything about it.
Standard English avoids double negatives: "don't ... nothing".
Use "don't ... anything" or "know nothing".
The other options lack "do" or add -s wrongly.

units.title: Linking words & cohesive devices
units.intro: Linking words (cohesive devices) join ideas: addition, contrast, cause and purpose. Each one has its own grammar. (This unit was Unit 8 before; Unit 8 now follows Textbook Unit 8.)

cards.title: Contrast and purpose
rule: although/even though + S + V.
despite/in spite of + noun / V-ing.
so that + S + modal; in order to + Vbase.

examples.fix: Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed.

examples.text: He revised so that he could pass.

cards.title: Connectors and the structures that follow them
body: **Contrast:** although / even though / though + clause; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing; however / nevertheless + new clause (after ; or .); whereas / while for direct comparison.
**Purpose:** to / in order to / so as to + base verb; so that + clause (often with can/could/would).
**Result:** so (after a comma); therefore / consequently / as a result (after ; or .); such + noun + that; so + adjective + that.
**Addition:** and; moreover / furthermore / in addition (after ; or .); not only ... but also.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Despite he studied, he failed."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** although/even though + S + V.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Despite he studied, he failed." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed."
**Check:** despite/in spite of + noun / V-ing.

cards.answer: Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed.

cards.title: Step by step: Linking words of contrast and purpose
body: **Step 1:** Although / even though / though + subject + verb: "Although it rained, we played."
**Step 2:** Despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: "Despite the rain, we played." / "In spite of being tired, she worked."
**Step 3:** However / nevertheless start a new sentence or follow a semicolon and take a comma: "It rained; however, we played."
**Step 4:** Whereas / while compare two contrasting facts: "Asmara is cool, whereas Massawa is hot."
**Step 5:** Purpose: to / in order to / so as to + verb; so that + subject + can/could/will/would + verb; "in order not to" for negative purpose.

**Example:** Join: "He was ill. He went to school." → "Although he was ill, he went to school." / "Despite being ill, he went to school." / "He was ill; however, he went to school." Purpose: "She saved money so that she could buy a bicycle."

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Although has a clause, Despite has a noun"
body: A-C, D-N.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Never write "despite of" or "although…but". Use one contrast word per sentence.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She bought the dress __________ it was expensive.
cards.why: The sentence shows a contrast (concession). 'Although' is followed by a full clause (subject + verb: 'it was expensive'). 'Despite' and 'In spite of' would require a noun phrase.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The team was at full strength despite the injury of one of its players.

options.A: The team wasn't complete because one of its players was injured.
options.B: The team was at full strength in spite of the injury of one of its players.
options.C: The team was at full strength because of the injury of one of its players.
options.D: The team wasn't at full strength although none of its players was injured.
options.E: The team was at full strength despite the injury of many of its players.

cards.why:
**Analysis:** The original sentence uses "despite" to show a contrast. 
**Step 1:** "In spite of" is the exact synonym for "despite".
**Step 2:** Choice B maintains the exact meaning: even though someone was injured, the team was still strong. 
**Step 3:** Choice A says it was not complete (wrong), Choice C says injury caused the strength (wrong).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He ought to look forward to achieving his goal __________ the temporarily existing difficulties.
cards.why: The word **'despite'** is a preposition used to show contrast. It is followed by a noun phrase ('the temporarily existing difficulties'). 'Even though' would require a full clause.

cards.title: Conjunctive adverbs
rule: therefore / however / moreover join two clauses with a semicolon before and a comma after: *It rained; however, we played.*
Do not write Because… so… or Although… but… (double conjunction).
Match meaning: therefore=result, however=contrast, moreover=addition.

examples.text: Although she tried, but she failed.
examples.fix: Although she tried, she failed.

examples.text: The roads were blocked; however, buses ran.

cards.title: Punctuating conjunctive adverbs
body: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise) are **not** conjunctions. They cannot join two clauses with only a comma.
Correct patterns: *It rained; **however**, we played.* or *It rained. **However**, we played.* or inside the clause: *We, **however**, played.*
Wrong: ✗ *It rained, however we played.* (comma splice).
Use only one connector per link: ✗ *Although it rained, but we played* → *Although it rained, we played.*

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the clause which is connected correctly.

options.A: Because he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.B: Despite he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.C: In spite of he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.D: Since he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.E: Although he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.

cards.why: The sentence shows a contrast (never tried it vs. very good at it). 'Although' is a conjunction followed by a full clause (subject + verb). 'Despite' and 'In spite of' must be followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

options.A: The exam was difficult; nevertheless, most students passed.
options.B: The exam was difficult, nevertheless most students passed.
options.C: The exam was difficult nevertheless, most students passed.
options.D: The exam was difficult; nevertheless most students, passed.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "nevertheless" is a conjunctive adverb.

**Step 2:** It needs a semicolon (or full stop) before it and a comma after it.

**Step 3:** Only the first option follows this pattern.

**Tip:** Check both meaning (contrast, result, addition, purpose) and structure: although + clause; despite + noun/-ing; so that + clause; in order to + verb; ; however, + clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "She practised every day; ____, she won the competition."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Winning was a result of practising every day.

**Step 2:** "as a result" introduces a consequence.

**Step 3:** The others show contrast, example or condition.

**Tip:** Check both meaning (contrast, result, addition, purpose) and structure: although + clause; despite + noun/-ing; so that + clause; in order to + verb; ; however, + clause.

'Although' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses. In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.
Students often choose 'but' (Option A) because in Tigrinya, it is natural to pair concession with contrast (e.g., 'ድኻ እኳ እንተኾነ፡ ግን...'). Option D is correct because no extra connector is allowed.

The sentence expresses a negative condition: we won't finish *unless* (if not) everyone works harder. This requires the negative conditional conjunction 'unless' (unless = if + not).

Students often choose 'if' (Option A) because they translate 'እንድሕር' directly. However, using 'if' would mean 'if everyone works harder, we won't finish', which is logically incorrect. Option B 'unless' is correct.
